# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutical Organic Chemistry I is a writing-and-drawing subject: most marks go to correct structures, correct names, and mechanisms drawn step by step with arrows. Study one unit a day: read the notes, redraw every mechanism and equation from memory on rough paper, name the examples without looking, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers. Pharmaceutical Organic Chemistry II (BP301T, semester 3) continues from here with benzene, phenols, aromatic amines and acids, fats and oils, polynuclear hydrocarbons and cycloalkanes, so those topics appear here only as short cross-references.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with mechanism, equations and examples.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**How the units follow the syllabus.** The five units match the five PCI units one to one. Unit 1 also has a short "toolkit" section (electronic effects and reaction intermediates) because the syllabus scope mentions intermediates and every later mechanism uses them. Unit 3 joins two syllabus headings (alkyl halides and alcohols), and Unit 5 joins carboxylic acids with aliphatic amines, exactly as the syllabus does.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Nomenclature and isomerism | IUPAC naming of given structures (and drawing structures from names), types of structural isomerism with examples, classification of organic compounds |
| 2 Alkanes, alkenes, dienes | E1 vs E2 with mechanism and kinetics, Saytzeff rule, Markownikoff and anti-Markownikoff (peroxide effect), ozonolysis, Diels–Alder, 1,2- vs 1,4-addition, stability of alkenes and dienes, halogenation of alkanes |
| 3 Alkyl halides and alcohols | SN1 vs SN2 (mechanism, kinetics, stereochemistry, factors), chloroform and iodoform, tests for alcohols (Lucas), uses of glycerol, chlorobutanol, benzyl alcohol |
| 4 Carbonyl compounds | Aldol, Cannizzaro (and crossed), benzoin, Perkin mechanisms; nucleophilic addition; electromeric effect; tests for aldehydes and ketones; uses of formaldehyde, hexamine, chloral hydrate, vanillin |
| 5 Acids and amines | Acidity and effect of substituents (inductive effect), basicity of aliphatic amines, tests for acids, esters and amides, structure and uses of aspirin, methyl salicylate, citric and lactic acid |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Mechanisms:** number each step, show where every electron pair moves with a curved arrow (on paper) or →, mark the slow step, name the intermediate (carbocation, carbanion, free radical, enolate) and finish with the product. Examiners give a mark per correct step.
2. **Kinetics line:** for SN1/SN2 and E1/E2 always write the rate law (rate = k[RX] or k[RX][Nu]) — it is a quick, sure mark.
3. **Named reactions:** write the general equation, one specific example with reagents and conditions on the arrow (dilute vs concentrated NaOH, temperature, catalyst), the mechanism if asked, and one or two uses.
4. **Starred compounds:** the syllabus asks for nomenclature, **two methods of preparation, two reactions and uses** for alkanes, alkenes, dienes, alkyl halides, alcohols, carbonyl compounds, acids and amines. Learn the tables in each unit in that shape.
5. **"Structure and uses" questions:** draw the full structure, give the IUPAC name, one preparation and three or four uses with a drug link (e.g. chlorobutanol as an injection preservative, hexamine as a urinary antiseptic).
6. **Nomenclature questions:** show your working — circle the parent chain, number it, then list prefixes alphabetically. Partial marks are given for the correct parent and numbering even if one prefix slips.
7. **Comparison questions** (SN1 vs SN2, E1 vs E2, inductive vs electromeric): use a table of at least six points.
8. **Order questions** (acidity, basicity, reactivity): write the order, then the reason (inductive, resonance, steric, solvation) in one line each.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five topics with full mechanisms: **SN1 vs SN2**, **E1 vs E2 with Saytzeff's rule**, **Markownikoff and the peroxide effect**, **aldol + Cannizzaro**, and **acidity of acids / basicity of amines**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions. Then spend ten minutes naming structures.

**Mechanisms in one line each**

| Reaction | Key steps | Rate law / feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free radical halogenation | Initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl·), propagation (Cl· + RH → HCl + R·; R· + Cl2 → RCl + Cl·), termination | 3° H > 2° > 1° |
| Electrophilic addition of HX | H⁺ adds → more stable carbocation → X⁻ adds | Markownikoff |
| Peroxide effect (HBr only) | RO· + HBr → Br·; Br· adds to give more stable radical; radical takes H from HBr | Anti-Markownikoff |
| Br2 addition | Cyclic bromonium ion, back attack by Br⁻ | Anti addition |
| E2 | One step, base removes β-H as X leaves | rate = k[RX][B]; anti-periplanar; no rearrangement |
| E1 | Slow ionisation to carbocation, then loss of β-H | rate = k[RX]; rearrangement possible |
| SN2 | One step, backside attack, pentacoordinate transition state | rate = k[RX][Nu]; inversion; CH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° |
| SN1 | Slow ionisation to planar carbocation, fast attack | rate = k[RX]; racemisation; 3° > 2° > 1° |
| Aldol | OH⁻ forms enolate → adds to C=O → protonation → (heat) dehydration | Needs α-H, dilute alkali |
| Cannizzaro | OH⁻ adds → hydride transfer to second aldehyde → proton exchange | No α-H, concentrated alkali |
| Benzoin | CN⁻ adds → carbanion → attacks second ArCHO → CN⁻ leaves | KCN catalyst, aromatic aldehydes |
| Perkin | Acetate makes anhydride carbanion → adds to ArCHO → elimination → hydrolysis | Gives cinnamic acid |
| Diels–Alder | Diene (s-cis) + dienophile in one concerted step | Gives cyclohexene; syn, stereospecific |

**Named reactions and their one-line meaning**

| Name | Reagents | Result | Unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wurtz | 2 RX + 2 Na, dry ether | R–R | 2 |
| Kolbe electrolysis | RCOONa, electrolysis | R–R | 2 |
| Sabatier–Senderens | Alkene + H2, Ni, about 250 °C | Alkane | 2 |
| Ozonolysis | O3, then Zn / H2O | Aldehydes / ketones | 2 |
| Kharasch (peroxide) effect | HBr + ROOR | Anti-Markownikoff bromide | 2 |
| Diels–Alder | Diene + dienophile, heat | Cyclohexene | 2 |
| Darzens | ROH + SOCl2, pyridine | RCl (pure) | 3 |
| Finkelstein | RCl + NaI in acetone | RI | 3 |
| Swarts | RBr + AgF | RF | 3 |
| Williamson | RX + R'ONa | Ether | 3 |
| Lucas test | Conc. HCl + ZnCl2 | 3° instant, 2° about 5 minutes, 1° none | 3 |
| Haloform (iodoform) | I2 + NaOH | CHI3 from CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– | 3 |
| Rosenmund | RCOCl + H2, Pd / BaSO4 | RCHO | 4 |
| Claisen–Schmidt | ArCHO + CH3CHO, dil. NaOH | Cinnamaldehyde | 4 |
| Crossed Cannizzaro | ArCHO + HCHO, conc. NaOH | ArCH2OH + HCOONa | 4 |
| Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky | RCH2COOH + Br2, red P | α-Bromo acid | 5 |
| Hofmann bromamide | RCONH2 + Br2 + NaOH | RNH2 (one C fewer) | 5 |
| Gabriel | K-phthalimide + RX, hydrolysis | Pure 1° amine | 5 |
| Carbylamine | 1° amine + CHCl3 + alc. KOH | Foul isocyanide | 5 |
| Hinsberg | C6H5SO2Cl + KOH | Separates 1°, 2°, 3° amines | 5 |

**Orders worth memorising**

| What | Order |
| --- | --- |
| Carbocation / free radical stability | 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3 (allyl, benzyl high) |
| Carbanion stability | CH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° |
| Alkene stability | tetra > tri > di (trans > cis) > mono > ethene |
| Halogen reactivity in halogenation | F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 |
| Leaving group | I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ |
| Carbonyl reactivity | HCHO > CH3CHO > CH3COCH3 > aromatic |
| Acidity | Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH > HCOOH > CH3COOH > phenol > water > ethanol |
| Basicity (methyl, in water) | (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 > amides (neutral) |
| Basicity (ethyl, in water) | (C2H5)2NH > (C2H5)3N > C2H5NH2 > NH3 |
| IUPAC priority | acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine |

**Numbers worth memorising**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| sp3 / sp2 bond angle | 109°28′ / 120° |
| C–C / C=C / butadiene C2–C3 | 1.54 / 1.34 / 1.48 Å |
| Delocalisation energy of buta-1,3-diene | about 3.5 kcal/mol |
| Chlorination rate per H, 3° : 2° : 1° | about 5 : 3.8 : 1 |
| pKa: acetic / formic / chloroacetic / trichloroacetic | 4.76 / 3.75 / 2.86 / 0.65 |
| pKb: NH3 / methylamine / dimethylamine / trimethylamine | 4.75 / 3.4 / 3.3 / 4.2 |
| Formalin | about 37–40% HCHO in water |
| Isomer counts | C4H10 = 2, C5H12 = 3, C6H14 = 5, C7H16 = 9, C4H10O = 7, C4H9Cl = 4 |

**Common traps in MCQs**

- The peroxide effect works **only with HBr**, not HCl or HI.
- SN2 gives **inversion**; SN1 gives **racemisation**; rearrangement only in SN1/E1.
- Aldehydes **with** α-H → aldol; **without** α-H → Cannizzaro. Formaldehyde, benzaldehyde and trimethylacetaldehyde have no α-H.
- In crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO, **formaldehyde is oxidised**, the other aldehyde is reduced.
- Benzaldehyde gives Tollens' test but usually **not** Fehling's test.
- Methanol gives a **negative** iodoform test; ethanol and propan-2-ol are positive.
- Benzyl alcohol is an alcohol, **not** a phenol (no FeCl3 colour).
- Amphetamine is a **primary** amine; amides are **not** basic.
- 2° aliphatic amines are the strongest bases in water, not 3°.
- Formic acid reduces Tollens' reagent; acetic acid does not.

**Drug links examiners like**

| Chemistry topic | Drug or product |
| --- | --- |
| Paraffins | Liquid paraffin (laxative), soft paraffin (ointment base) |
| Halogenated compounds | Ethyl chloride spray, iodoform antiseptic, chloroform water |
| Alcohols | Ethanol 70% antiseptic, chlorobutanol and benzyl alcohol preservatives, glycerol humectant, propylene glycol cosolvent, cetostearyl alcohol in creams |
| Glycerol → glyceryl trinitrate | Angina |
| Formaldehyde + ammonia → hexamine | Urinary antiseptic |
| Acetaldehyde trimer | Paraldehyde (anticonvulsant) |
| Benzoin → benzil + urea | Phenytoin |
| Salicylic acid esters | Aspirin (analgesic, antiplatelet), methyl salicylate (counter-irritant) |
| Benzyl benzoate | Scabies |
| Citric / tartaric acid + NaHCO3 | Effervescent granules |
| Ethylenediamine | Aminophylline |

# Preliminary tests on an unknown organic compound

**Aim:** To record the physical state, colour and odour of an unknown organic compound and to find out whether it is aliphatic or aromatic and saturated or unsaturated.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Never taste an unknown, smell it only by wafting, and keep flammable liquids away from flames.

## Principle

Simple observations narrow down the class of an unknown before chemical tests are done:

- **Colour and odour** point to certain groups (yellow nitro compounds, fruity esters, carbolic phenol).
- **Ignition test:** aromatic compounds have a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio and burn with a **sooty, smoky flame**; aliphatic compounds burn with a clean, non-smoky flame. Carbohydrates char with a smell of burnt sugar.
- **Unsaturation:** C=C and C≡C bonds add bromine (red-brown colour disappears) and are oxidised by cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent; purple colour disappears and brown MnO2 forms).

## Requirements

Unknown compound, spatula, porcelain tile or crucible lid, burner, test tubes, 5% bromine in carbon tetrachloride (or bromine water), 1% aqueous KMnO4 with a little sodium carbonate (Baeyer's reagent), litmus papers.

## Procedure

1. **Physical state:** note whether the compound is a crystalline solid, an amorphous powder or a liquid.
2. **Colour:** observe in daylight against white paper.
3. **Odour:** waft the vapour gently towards the nose.
4. **Ignition test:** place about 0.1 g (or 2 drops) on a porcelain tile or crucible lid and heat in the flame. Note the type of flame and any residue.
5. **Bromine test:** dissolve about 0.1 g in 1 ml of CCl4 (or water if soluble) and add the bromine solution drop by drop with shaking.
6. **Baeyer's test:** dissolve about 0.1 g in 2 ml of water or acetone and add Baeyer's reagent drop by drop with shaking.
7. **Litmus:** test an aqueous solution or suspension with blue and red litmus.

## Observations

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical state / colour | Yellow liquid | Possibly a nitro compound |
| Colour | Colourless liquid turning brown on standing | Possibly aniline (air oxidation) |
| Odour | Fruity | Ester |
| Odour | Bitter almond | Benzaldehyde or nitrobenzene |
| Odour | Carbolic (phenolic) | Phenol |
| Odour | Fishy / ammoniacal | Amine |
| Odour | Vinegar-like | Acetic acid |
| Ignition | Sooty, smoky flame | Aromatic compound |
| Ignition | Non-smoky, clean flame | Aliphatic compound |
| Ignition | Chars, smell of burnt sugar | Carbohydrate |
| Ignition | White residue left | Salt of an acid (e.g. sodium benzoate) |
| Bromine | Red-brown colour discharged, no fumes | Unsaturated (C=C) |
| Bromine | Colour discharged with white precipitate | Phenol or aromatic amine (substitution) |
| Baeyer's | Purple → brown precipitate | Unsaturation (or easily oxidised groups: aldehydes, phenols) |
| Litmus | Blue → red | Acidic compound (acid, phenol) |
| Litmus | Red → blue | Basic compound (amine) |

**Worked record (example).** White crystals, odourless, sooty flame, no change with bromine or Baeyer's reagent, blue litmus turns red → aromatic, saturated, acidic compound; go on to element detection and the acid tests.

## Result

The given compound is a ___ (solid/liquid), ___ (aromatic/aliphatic), ___ (saturated/unsaturated) compound of ___ nature.

## Precautions

1. Use only a small amount in the ignition test; some compounds burn violently.
2. Smell by wafting, never by sniffing directly.
3. Baeyer's test is not specific: aldehydes, phenols and formic acid also reduce KMnO4, so confirm with the bromine test.
4. Bromine in CCl4 is toxic and corrosive; use it in a fume hood.

## Viva questions

1. **Why do aromatic compounds burn with a sooty flame?** Their high carbon content leaves unburnt carbon particles.
2. **What is Baeyer's reagent?** 1% cold dilute alkaline potassium permanganate.
3. **Why does phenol decolourise bromine water?** It undergoes ring substitution to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
4. **Why does aniline darken on standing?** It is slowly oxidised by air to coloured products.
5. **What does a residue after ignition indicate?** The compound is a metal salt (e.g. a sodium salt of an acid).
6. **Why are preliminary tests only indicative?** Several classes give the same response; they guide, not confirm.

# Detection of nitrogen, sulphur and halogens (Lassaigne's test)

**Aim:** To detect nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in the given organic compound by Lassaigne's sodium fusion test.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Sodium reacts violently with water: handle it with forceps, keep it under kerosene, and wear goggles during fusion.

## Principle

In organic compounds N, S and halogens are covalently bonded and do not give ionic tests. Fusing the compound with metallic sodium converts them into water-soluble **ionic sodium salts**:

```text
   Na + C + N  ──fusion──▶  NaCN
   2 Na + S    ──fusion──▶  Na2S
   Na + X      ──fusion──▶  NaX     (X = Cl, Br, I)
   Na + C + N + S ──────▶  NaSCN    (if N and S both present and sodium is limited)
```

The aqueous extract of the fused mass (**Lassaigne's extract** or sodium fusion extract) is then tested for CN⁻, S²⁻ and X⁻.

## Requirements

Sodium metal, fusion (ignition) tubes, china dish, distilled water, filter paper, freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution, ferric chloride solution, dilute H2SO4, sodium nitroprusside solution, lead acetate solution, acetic acid, dilute HNO3, silver nitrate solution, dilute ammonia.

## Procedure

**A. Preparation of Lassaigne's extract**

1. Dry a small pea-sized piece of sodium between filter papers and place it in a clean fusion tube.
2. Heat gently until the sodium melts to a shiny globule.
3. Add a small amount (about 50 mg, or 2 drops) of the compound and heat, first gently, then strongly until the tube is red hot.
4. Plunge the red-hot tube into about 10 ml of distilled water in a china dish (cover the dish with a wire gauze; the tube shatters).
5. Crush the glass, boil the contents for a few minutes and filter. The clear, colourless filtrate is Lassaigne's extract.

**B. Test for nitrogen**

6. To 2 ml of extract add 1 ml of freshly prepared FeSO4 solution, boil, cool, add 2 drops of FeCl3 and acidify with dilute H2SO4. A **Prussian blue** colour or precipitate shows nitrogen.

**C. Test for sulphur**

7. To 1 ml of extract add a few drops of sodium nitroprusside: a **violet/purple** colour shows sulphur.
8. Acidify 1 ml of extract with acetic acid and add lead acetate: a **black precipitate** (PbS) confirms sulphur.

**D. Test for N and S together**

9. To 1 ml of extract add dilute HCl and FeCl3: a **blood-red** colour (Fe(SCN)3) shows both N and S. (In this case the Prussian blue test may fail.)

**E. Test for halogens**

10. Acidify 2 ml of extract with dilute HNO3 and boil for a few minutes (this removes CN⁻ as HCN and S²⁻ as H2S, which would otherwise give precipitates with AgNO3).
11. Cool and add AgNO3 solution. Observe the precipitate and test its solubility in dilute ammonia.

## Observations

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FeSO4 + FeCl3 + H2SO4 | Prussian blue | N present (NaCN → Na4[Fe(CN)6] → Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3) |
| Sodium nitroprusside | Violet | S present (Na4[Fe(CN)5NOS]) |
| Lead acetate | Black precipitate | S present (PbS) |
| FeCl3 + HCl | Blood red | N and S both (Fe(SCN)3) |
| AgNO3 | White curdy precipitate, soluble in ammonia | Cl present |
| AgNO3 | Pale yellow precipitate, sparingly soluble in ammonia | Br present |
| AgNO3 | Yellow precipitate, insoluble in ammonia | I present |

**Chemistry of the nitrogen test**

```text
   FeSO4 + 2 NaOH → Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
   6 NaCN + Fe(OH)2 → Na4[Fe(CN)6] + 2 NaOH
   3 Na4[Fe(CN)6] + 4 Fe³⁺ → Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (Prussian blue) + 12 Na⁺
```

**Worked record (example).** Extract gives Prussian blue, no colour with nitroprusside, white precipitate with AgNO3 soluble in ammonia → the compound contains **nitrogen and chlorine** but no sulphur.

## Result

The given compound contains ___ (N / S / Cl / Br / I) and does not contain ___.

## Precautions

1. Use clean, dry sodium and a dry tube; water causes explosions.
2. Heat the tube to red heat so that fusion is complete.
3. Use freshly prepared FeSO4 (old solutions are oxidised).
4. Boil with HNO3 before the halogen test to avoid false precipitates from CN⁻ and S²⁻.
5. Do not use excess compound; it gives a dark, charred extract.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is sodium used?** It is highly reactive and converts covalent N, S and X into ionic salts.
2. **Why is the extract boiled with HNO3 before adding AgNO3?** To decompose NaCN and Na2S, which would also precipitate with AgNO3.
3. **Why can the nitrogen test fail when S is also present?** NaSCN forms instead of NaCN, giving a blood-red colour with FeCl3, not Prussian blue.
4. **What is the formula of Prussian blue?** Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3, ferric ferrocyanide.
5. **Why does hydrazine not respond to Lassaigne's test for nitrogen?** It has no carbon, so NaCN cannot form.
6. **How are Cl, Br and I distinguished?** By the colour of the silver halide and its solubility in ammonia.
practicals.title: Detection of N, S and halogens (Lassaigne's test)

# Solubility tests and solubility classification

**Aim:** To place the given organic compound in a solubility group using water, dilute alkalis, dilute acid and concentrated sulphuric acid.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Add concentrated H2SO4 slowly; it may heat up and char the compound.

## Principle

"Like dissolves like." Small polar molecules dissolve in water. Water-insoluble **acids** dissolve in alkali because they form salts; water-insoluble **bases** dissolve in dilute acid for the same reason. Concentrated H2SO4 dissolves neutral compounds that contain oxygen or a C=C, because it protonates them. Hydrocarbons and their halogen derivatives dissolve in none of these.

```text
   R–COOH + NaHCO3 → R–COONa (soluble) + H2O + CO2↑        (strong acids only)
   ArOH  + NaOH   → ArONa (soluble) + H2O                 (phenols: NaOH yes, NaHCO3 no)
   R–NH2 + HCl    → R–NH3⁺ Cl⁻ (soluble)
```

## Requirements

Unknown compound, test tubes, distilled water, 5% NaOH, 5% NaHCO3, 5% HCl, concentrated H2SO4, litmus paper, dilute HCl and dilute NaOH for reprecipitation.

## Procedure

1. **Water:** shake about 0.1 g (or 0.2 ml) with 3 ml of water. If it dissolves, test the solution with litmus.
2. **5% NaOH:** if insoluble in water, shake a fresh portion with 3 ml of 5% NaOH. If it dissolves, acidify with dilute HCl: reprecipitation confirms an acidic compound.
3. **5% NaHCO3:** if soluble in NaOH, try a fresh portion with 5% NaHCO3. Note effervescence.
4. **5% HCl:** if insoluble in water and NaOH, shake with 3 ml of 5% HCl. If it dissolves, make alkaline with NaOH: reprecipitation confirms a base.
5. **Conc. H2SO4:** if insoluble in all the above, add the compound to 1 ml of cold concentrated H2SO4. Note dissolution, colour change or warming.

## Observations

```text
                           Compound + water
                ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
             Soluble                         Insoluble
         test with litmus                        │
   ┌──────────┼─────────────┐              5% NaOH
 acidic     basic        neutral        ┌──────┴────────┐
 (lower     (lower      (alcohols,    soluble        insoluble
 acids,     amines)     aldehydes,       │               │
 some                   ketones,     5% NaHCO3        5% HCl
 phenols)               sugars,     ┌────┴────┐     ┌────┴─────┐
                        urea)     soluble  insoluble soluble   insoluble
                                  (CO2)              (amines,      │
                                  carboxylic phenols  aniline)  conc. H2SO4
                                  acids                       ┌────┴─────┐
                                                           soluble     insoluble
                                                           (neutral    (hydrocarbons,
                                                           O-containing halogenated
                                                           compounds,  hydrocarbons)
                                                           alkenes)
```

| Unknown (example) | Water | NaOH | NaHCO3 | HCl | Conc. H2SO4 | Group |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Benzoic acid | Insoluble (cold) | Soluble | Soluble, effervescence | — | — | Carboxylic acid |
| β-Naphthol | Insoluble | Soluble | Insoluble | — | — | Phenol |
| Aniline | Insoluble | Insoluble | — | Soluble | — | Base (amine) |
| Methyl salicylate | Insoluble | Soluble (phenolic –OH) | Insoluble | — | — | Phenolic ester |
| Benzaldehyde | Insoluble | Insoluble | — | Insoluble | Soluble | Neutral, oxygen-containing |
| Chlorobenzene / toluene | Insoluble | Insoluble | — | Insoluble | Insoluble | Inert (hydrocarbon or aryl halide) |
| Glucose / urea | Soluble, neutral | — | — | — | — | Water-soluble neutral |

## Result

The given compound belongs to the ___ solubility group, indicating a ___ (acid / phenol / base / neutral / inert) compound.

## Precautions

1. Use small amounts so that solubility is easy to judge.
2. Always use a fresh portion of compound for each solvent.
3. Confirm acid or base solubility by reprecipitation.
4. Add conc. H2SO4 to the compound slowly and cool if needed.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does benzoic acid dissolve in NaHCO3 but phenol does not?** Benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is stronger than carbonic acid; phenol (pKa 10) is weaker.
2. **Why does aniline dissolve in dilute HCl?** It forms the water-soluble salt anilinium chloride.
3. **Why do lower alcohols dissolve in water?** They form hydrogen bonds with water.
4. **Which compounds dissolve in concentrated H2SO4 only?** Neutral compounds containing oxygen (aldehydes, ketones, esters, ethers, higher alcohols) and alkenes.
5. **What is the use of solubility tests?** They narrow down the functional group and decide which group tests to perform.
6. **Why is reprecipitation done?** To prove that the compound dissolved by salt formation and not merely by physical solubility.

# Functional group tests for carboxylic acids and phenols

**Aim:** To detect a carboxylic acid group or a phenolic group in the given organic compound.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Phenols burn the skin; wash any spill at once with plenty of water.

## Principle

- **Carboxylic acids** (pKa about 4–5) are stronger than carbonic acid, so they release CO2 from sodium bicarbonate. With an alcohol and acid catalyst they form sweet-smelling esters. Their neutral salts give characteristic colours or precipitates with ferric chloride.
- **Phenols** are weaker acids (pKa about 10): they dissolve in NaOH but not NaHCO3. The –OH on the ring forms coloured complexes with Fe³⁺ and activates the ring, so bromine substitutes at once.

## Requirements

Unknown compound, saturated NaHCO3, ethanol, conc. H2SO4, neutral FeCl3 (FeCl3 solution to which dilute NaOH is added until a faint permanent precipitate forms, then filtered), dilute ammonia, bromine water, NaNO2, phthalic anhydride, 10% NaOH, test tubes, water bath.

To prepare a **neutral solution** of an acid for the FeCl3 test: dissolve a little acid in dilute ammonia, boil off the excess ammonia, cool.

## Procedure

**Carboxylic acid**

1. **Bicarbonate test:** add a little compound to 2 ml of saturated NaHCO3. Brisk effervescence (CO2, turns lime water milky) shows –COOH.
2. **Ester test:** warm 0.1 g of the acid with 1 ml of ethanol and 2 drops of conc. H2SO4 on a water bath for 5 minutes; pour into a beaker of cold water. A **fruity smell** shows an acid.
3. **Neutral FeCl3 test:** add neutral FeCl3 to the neutral solution of the acid.

**Phenol**

4. **FeCl3 test:** add 2 drops of neutral FeCl3 to a dilute aqueous or alcoholic solution of the compound. A violet, blue, green or red colour shows a phenol (or enol).
5. **Bromine water:** add bromine water drop by drop to an aqueous solution; decolourisation with a white precipitate (e.g. 2,4,6-tribromophenol) shows a phenol.
6. **Liebermann's nitroso test:** dissolve a crystal of NaNO2 in 1 ml of conc. H2SO4, add a little phenol and warm gently: a deep green or blue colour forms; pour into water → red; make alkaline with NaOH → green or blue again.
7. **Phthalein test:** heat a little phenol with an equal amount of phthalic anhydride and 2 drops of conc. H2SO4 for 1 minute; cool, pour into dilute NaOH: phenol gives a **pink/red** colour (phenolphthalein).

## Observations

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NaHCO3 | Brisk effervescence | Carboxylic acid present |
| Ester test | Fruity odour | Carboxylic acid present |
| Neutral FeCl3 on acid | Buff precipitate | Benzoate |
| Neutral FeCl3 on acid | Violet colour | Salicylate (phenolic –OH as well) |
| Neutral FeCl3 on acid | Deep red colour, brown-red precipitate on boiling | Acetate or formate |
| Neutral FeCl3 on acid | Brownish precipitate | Succinate |
| FeCl3 on phenol | Violet | Phenol |
| FeCl3 on phenol | Green or greenish | β-Naphthol |
| Bromine water | White precipitate | Phenol (tribromophenol) |
| Liebermann's test | Green/blue → red (water) → blue/green (alkali) | Phenol |
| Phthalein test | Pink/red in alkali | Phenol |

**Worked record (example).** White solid; NaHCO3 effervescence; ester test fruity; neutral FeCl3 violet → carboxylic acid with a free phenolic –OH (salicylic acid likely; confirm by melting point, about 158 °C).

## Result

The given compound contains a ___ (carboxylic acid / phenolic) group.

## Precautions

1. Use **neutral** FeCl3; free acid or alkali spoils the colours.
2. Remove all excess ammonia before the FeCl3 test on acids.
3. Some phenols (e.g. hindered phenols) give weak FeCl3 colours; confirm with another test.
4. Handle conc. H2SO4 and bromine water carefully.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does phenol not effervesce with NaHCO3?** It is a weaker acid than carbonic acid.
2. **What is formed in the ester test with acetic acid and ethanol?** Ethyl acetate.
3. **Why does salicylic acid give a violet colour with FeCl3?** It has a free phenolic –OH, which complexes iron.
4. **Why does aspirin not give an immediate violet colour?** Its phenolic –OH is acetylated; colour appears only after hydrolysis.
5. **What is the white precipitate formed by phenol with bromine water?** 2,4,6-Tribromophenol.
6. **Which other compounds give a colour with FeCl3?** Enols such as ethyl acetoacetate.
practicals.title: Functional group tests: carboxylic acids and phenols

# Functional group tests for aldehydes and ketones

**Aim:** To detect a carbonyl group in the given compound and to decide whether it is an aldehyde or a ketone.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Tollens' reagent must be made fresh and discarded at once after use (on standing it can form explosive silver compounds).

## Principle

- **2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP)** condenses with any >C=O to give a coloured, insoluble hydrazone: R2C=O + H2N–NH–Ar → R2C=N–NH–Ar + H2O.
- **Aldehydes are reducing agents**; ketones are not. Aldehydes reduce Ag⁺ to silver (Tollens') and Cu²⁺ to Cu2O (Fehling's, Benedict's), and restore the colour of Schiff's reagent.
- **Methyl ketones** give a red colour with sodium nitroprusside in alkali and yellow iodoform with I2/NaOH.

```text
   R–CHO + 2 [Ag(NH3)2]⁺ + 3 OH⁻ → R–COO⁻ + 2 Ag↓ + 4 NH3 + 2 H2O     (silver mirror)
   R–CHO + 2 Cu²⁺ + 5 OH⁻ → R–COO⁻ + Cu2O↓ (red) + 3 H2O              (Fehling's)
```

## Requirements

Unknown compound, 2,4-DNP reagent (Brady's reagent), Tollens' reagent (AgNO3 + a drop of NaOH, then dilute ammonia just to dissolve the precipitate), Fehling's solutions A and B, Schiff's reagent, sodium nitroprusside solution, NaOH, iodine in KI, ethanol, water bath.

## Procedure

1. **2,4-DNP test:** dissolve a drop or a few crystals of the compound in 1 ml of ethanol; add 2 ml of Brady's reagent and shake. A yellow, orange or red precipitate shows a carbonyl group.
2. **Tollens' test:** to 2 ml of freshly prepared Tollens' reagent in a clean test tube add 2–3 drops of the compound; warm on a water bath (about 60 °C) for a few minutes. A silver mirror or black precipitate shows an aldehyde.
3. **Fehling's test:** mix 1 ml each of Fehling's A and B, add the compound and boil for 2 minutes. A red-brown precipitate shows an aliphatic aldehyde (or reducing sugar).
4. **Schiff's test:** add the compound to 1 ml of Schiff's reagent and shake in the cold. A pink/magenta colour shows an aldehyde.
5. **Sodium nitroprusside test:** to the compound add 1 ml of sodium nitroprusside solution and make alkaline with NaOH. A red/wine-red colour shows a methyl ketone (acetone).
6. **Iodoform test:** to 0.2 ml of compound in 2 ml of water add 2 ml of 10% NaOH, then iodine solution drop by drop with warming until a faint brown colour remains. A yellow precipitate with a characteristic smell (CHI3) shows CH3CO– (or CH3CH(OH)–).

## Observations

| Test | Aldehyde (e.g. benzaldehyde / acetaldehyde) | Ketone (e.g. acetone) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2,4-DNP | Orange-red / yellow precipitate | Yellow-orange precipitate |
| Tollens' | Silver mirror | No change |
| Fehling's | Red Cu2O with acetaldehyde; benzaldehyde usually negative | No change |
| Schiff's | Pink/magenta | No colour |
| Nitroprusside + NaOH | No red colour | Red colour (acetone) |
| Iodoform | Positive only for acetaldehyde | Positive for methyl ketones |

**Worked record (example).** Colourless liquid with bitter-almond odour; orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP; silver mirror with Tollens'; Fehling's negative; Schiff's pink → aromatic aldehyde (benzaldehyde likely; boiling point about 178 °C; 2,4-DNP derivative melting point about 237 °C).

## Result

The given compound contains an ___ (aldehyde / ketone) group.

## Precautions

1. Clean the test tube with chromic acid or NaOH and rinse well before Tollens' test, or the mirror will not form.
2. Never heat Tollens' reagent directly over a flame; use a water bath and discard it immediately afterwards.
3. Mix Fehling's A and B only at the time of use.
4. Do the Schiff's test in the cold; heating restores the colour without any aldehyde.

## Viva questions

1. **What is Brady's reagent?** 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine in acid (sulphuric acid with ethanol/water).
2. **Why do ketones not respond to Tollens' test?** They have no H on the carbonyl carbon and are not easily oxidised.
3. **Why does benzaldehyde fail the Fehling's test?** Aromatic aldehydes are weaker reducing agents and generally do not reduce Fehling's solution.
4. **What does Rochelle salt do in Fehling's B?** Its tartrate complexes Cu²⁺ and keeps it in solution in alkali.
5. **What is Schiff's reagent?** A solution of rosaniline (magenta) decolourised by SO2.
6. **Which group does the iodoform test detect?** CH3–CO– or CH3–CH(OH)–.
practicals.title: Functional group tests: aldehydes and ketones

# Functional group tests for alcohols and esters

**Aim:** To detect an alcoholic –OH group or an ester group in the given compound, and to classify an alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Sodium reacts violently with water: use a dry sample and a tiny piece of sodium.

## Principle

- **Alcohols** release hydrogen with sodium, form coloured complexes with ceric ammonium nitrate, form fruity esters with acetic acid, and react with the Lucas reagent at rates that depend on carbocation stability (3° > 2° > 1°).
- **Esters** react with hydroxylamine in alkali to form **hydroxamic acids**, which give a red-violet ferric complex; they also consume alkali on warming (saponification).

```text
   2 R–OH + 2 Na → 2 R–ONa + H2↑
   R–OH + HCl ──ZnCl2──▶ R–Cl (insoluble, turbidity) + H2O
   R–COOR' + NH2OH ──NaOH──▶ R–CONHOH (hydroxamic acid) + R'OH
   3 R–CONHOH + Fe³⁺ → (R–CONHO)3Fe (red-violet) + 3 H⁺
```

## Requirements

Unknown compound (dry), sodium metal, ceric ammonium nitrate reagent, glacial acetic acid, conc. H2SO4, Lucas reagent (anhydrous ZnCl2 dissolved in conc. HCl), chromic acid (K2Cr2O7 in dilute H2SO4), iodine–KI, NaOH, hydroxylamine hydrochloride, dilute HCl, FeCl3 solution, phenolphthalein, test tubes, water bath.

## Procedure

**Alcohols**

1. **Sodium test:** add a small dry piece of sodium to 1 ml of the dry liquid. Effervescence (H2, burns with a pop) shows –OH.
2. **Ceric ammonium nitrate:** add 3–4 drops of the compound to 1 ml of the reagent. Yellow → red shows an alcohol.
3. **Ester formation:** warm 1 ml of compound with 1 ml of glacial acetic acid and 2 drops of conc. H2SO4 for 5 minutes; pour into cold water. Fruity smell shows an alcohol.
4. **Lucas test:** add 0.5 ml of compound to 2 ml of Lucas reagent at room temperature, shake and note the time for turbidity.
5. **Chromic acid test:** add 1 drop of compound to 1 ml of chromic acid. Orange → green shows a 1° or 2° alcohol.
6. **Iodoform test:** as in the carbonyl practical; positive for ethanol and propan-2-ol.

**Esters**

7. **Hydroxamic acid test:** warm 2 drops of the ester with 1 ml of 0.5 M hydroxylamine hydrochloride in ethanol and 0.5 ml of 6 M NaOH to boiling; cool, acidify with dilute HCl and add 2 drops of FeCl3. A red to violet colour shows an ester.
8. **Saponification test:** add 2 drops of phenolphthalein to 2 ml of dilute NaOH (pink); add the ester and warm on a water bath. The pink colour fades as the alkali is used up.
9. **Odour:** most simple esters have a fruity smell; methyl salicylate smells of wintergreen.

## Observations

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium | Effervescence of H2 | –OH present (alcohol, phenol or acid) |
| Ceric ammonium nitrate | Yellow → red | Alcohol |
| Acetic acid + H2SO4 | Fruity smell | Alcohol |
| Lucas | Turbidity at once | Tertiary alcohol |
| Lucas | Turbidity in about 5 minutes | Secondary alcohol |
| Lucas | No turbidity at room temperature | Primary alcohol |
| Chromic acid | Orange → green | 1° or 2° alcohol |
| Iodoform | Yellow precipitate | CH3CH(OH)– alcohol |
| Hydroxamic acid | Red-violet | Ester |
| NaOH + phenolphthalein, warm | Pink fades | Ester (saponified) |

**Worked record (example).** Colourless volatile liquid, burns with a non-smoky flame, soluble in water; effervescence with Na; CAN red; Lucas no turbidity; iodoform positive; boiling point about 78 °C → **ethanol**.

## Result

The given compound is a ___ (primary / secondary / tertiary) alcohol, or an ester.

## Precautions

1. The sample must be dry for the sodium test (water also gives H2).
2. Lucas test applies only to alcohols soluble in the reagent (up to about six carbons).
3. Acids and phenols must be ruled out first, since they also react with sodium.
4. Acidify before adding FeCl3 in the hydroxamic acid test (in alkali, iron precipitates as hydroxide).

## Viva questions

1. **What is the Lucas reagent?** Anhydrous zinc chloride in concentrated hydrochloric acid.
2. **Why do 3° alcohols react fastest in the Lucas test?** They form the most stable carbocation (SN1).
3. **Why do 3° alcohols not give the chromic acid test?** The carbon bearing –OH has no H to lose on oxidation.
4. **Name the coloured compound in the hydroxamic acid test.** Ferric hydroxamate.
5. **What is saponification?** Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester to a carboxylate salt and an alcohol.
6. **How is methanol distinguished from ethanol?** Methanol gives a negative iodoform test.
practicals.title: Functional group tests: alcohols and esters

# Functional group tests for amines, amides/urea, anilides and nitro compounds

**Aim:** To identify the nitrogen-containing functional group (amine, amide, urea, anilide or nitro) in a compound that gave a positive Lassaigne's test for nitrogen.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Isocyanides (carbylamine test) are very foul and toxic: do this test in a fume hood and destroy the product with conc. HCl.

## Principle

- **Amines** are basic (dissolve in dilute HCl). Primary amines give the carbylamine (isocyanide) reaction. **Primary aromatic amines** form diazonium salts at 0–5 °C, which couple with β-naphthol to give an orange-red azo dye.
- **Amides** release ammonia when boiled with alkali; **urea** forms biuret on gentle heating, which gives a violet colour with alkaline copper sulphate.
- **Anilides** (e.g. acetanilide) are amides of aniline: acid hydrolysis releases the primary aromatic amine, which then gives the azo dye test.
- **Nitro compounds** are reduced (Sn/HCl, or Zn/NH4Cl) to amines or hydroxylamines, which are then detected.

```text
   R–NH2 + CHCl3 + 3 KOH → R–N≡C (foul) + 3 KCl + 3 H2O
   C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2 HCl ──0–5 °C──▶ C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2 H2O
   C6H5N2⁺Cl⁻ + β-naphthol (in NaOH) → orange-red 1-phenylazo-2-naphthol
   R–CONH2 + NaOH → R–COONa + NH3↑
   2 NH2CONH2 ──heat──▶ NH2CONHCONH2 (biuret) + NH3
```

## Requirements

Unknown compound, dilute and conc. HCl, chloroform, alcoholic KOH, NaNO2, β-naphthol in NaOH, ice, 10% NaOH, red litmus, 1% CuSO4, 70% H2SO4 (or conc. HCl) for hydrolysis, granulated tin, zinc dust, ammonium chloride, Tollens' reagent, test tubes, water bath.

## Procedure

**Amines**

1. **Solubility:** dissolves in dilute HCl; reprecipitates with NaOH (aromatic amines such as aniline).
2. **Carbylamine test:** warm 2 drops of the amine with 3 drops of chloroform and 2 ml of alcoholic KOH. An offensive smell shows a 1° amine. Destroy the product with conc. HCl.
3. **Azo dye test (1° aromatic amines):** dissolve 2 drops of amine in 1 ml of dilute HCl, cool in ice; add ice-cold NaNO2 solution; pour into ice-cold alkaline β-naphthol. Orange-red precipitate shows a 1° aromatic amine.

**Amides and urea**

4. **NaOH test:** boil the compound with 10% NaOH; hold moist red litmus at the mouth. Smell of ammonia and blue litmus show an amide (or ammonium salt).
5. **Biuret test (urea):** heat a little urea gently in a dry tube until it melts and solidifies again; cool, dissolve in water, add NaOH and 1 drop of 1% CuSO4. Violet colour shows urea.
6. **Nitrous acid test (urea):** add NaNO2 and dilute HCl to an aqueous solution of urea: brisk effervescence of N2.

**Anilides**

7. **Hydrolysis:** reflux 0.5 g of the compound with 5 ml of 70% H2SO4 (or conc. HCl) for about 10 minutes. Note the smell of acetic acid. Cool, make the solution alkaline, and test a portion for a 1° aromatic amine by the azo dye test (step 3). Positive → anilide (acetanilide).

**Nitro compounds**

8. **Reduction test:** warm 0.5 ml of the compound with a few pieces of tin and 3 ml of conc. HCl for several minutes; decant, cool, and carry out the azo dye test on the solution. Orange-red dye shows an aromatic nitro compound (reduced to the amine).
9. **Mulliken–Barker test:** warm the compound with zinc dust and NH4Cl solution in ethanol; filter into Tollens' reagent. Grey/black precipitate (the hydroxylamine reduces Ag⁺) shows a nitro group.

## Observations

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dilute HCl | Dissolves; reprecipitates with NaOH | Amine (base) |
| Carbylamine | Offensive odour | 1° amine |
| Diazotisation + β-naphthol | Orange-red precipitate | 1° aromatic amine (aniline) |
| Boil with NaOH | NH3 evolved, red litmus blue | Amide |
| Biuret | Violet | Urea |
| NaNO2 + HCl on urea | Effervescence | Urea |
| Acid hydrolysis then azo dye | Acetic acid smell; orange-red dye | Anilide (acetanilide) |
| Sn/HCl then azo dye | Orange-red dye | Aromatic nitro compound |
| Mulliken–Barker | Grey/black silver | Nitro compound |

**Worked record (example).** White crystalline solid, neutral, N present; no NH3 with cold NaOH; on acid hydrolysis smell of acetic acid and positive azo dye test; melting point about 114 °C → **acetanilide**.

## Result

The nitrogen-containing group in the given compound is ___.

## Precautions

1. Keep diazotisation below 5 °C; diazonium salts decompose on warming.
2. Do the carbylamine test in the fume hood and destroy the isocyanide with acid.
3. For urea, heat gently; strong heating gives cyanuric acid instead of biuret.
4. Make sure the reduction with tin is complete before the azo dye test.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is diazotisation done at 0–5 °C?** Diazonium salts are unstable and decompose to phenols and N2 at higher temperatures.
2. **What colour is the azo dye from aniline and β-naphthol?** Orange-red.
3. **Why does acetanilide not give the azo dye test directly?** Its nitrogen is acylated; hydrolysis must first free aniline.
4. **Which amines give the carbylamine test?** Primary amines only (aliphatic and aromatic).
5. **What is formed when urea is heated gently?** Biuret and ammonia.
6. **How is nitrobenzene detected?** By reduction to aniline, then diazotisation and coupling.
practicals.title: Functional group tests: amines, amides/urea, anilides, nitro compounds

# Tests for carbohydrates

**Aim:** To detect a carbohydrate in the given compound and to distinguish glucose, fructose, sucrose, lactose and starch.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Add concentrated H2SO4 along the side of the tube slowly in the Molisch test.

## Principle

- **Molisch test (general):** concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates carbohydrates to furfural derivatives, which condense with α-naphthol to give a violet ring.
- **Reducing sugars** (glucose, fructose, lactose, maltose) have a free aldehyde or keto group (hemiacetal) and reduce Cu²⁺ (Fehling's, Benedict's). Sucrose is non-reducing.
- **Barfoed's test:** in mildly acidic copper acetate, monosaccharides reduce Cu²⁺ faster than disaccharides.
- **Seliwanoff's test:** ketoses (fructose) dehydrate quickly in HCl to hydroxymethylfurfural, which gives a cherry-red colour with resorcinol.
- **Iodine test:** starch forms a blue-black complex with iodine.
- **Osazone test:** reducing sugars heated with phenylhydrazine form crystalline osazones of characteristic shape and time of formation.

## Requirements

Sugar samples, Molisch reagent (α-naphthol in ethanol), conc. H2SO4, Fehling's A and B, Benedict's reagent, Barfoed's reagent, Seliwanoff's reagent (resorcinol in HCl), iodine solution, phenylhydrazine hydrochloride, sodium acetate, boiling water bath, microscope.

## Procedure

1. **Molisch test:** to 2 ml of sugar solution add 2 drops of Molisch reagent; pour 1 ml of conc. H2SO4 slowly down the side of the tube. A violet ring at the junction shows a carbohydrate.
2. **Fehling's / Benedict's test:** boil 2 ml of the sugar solution with 2 ml of mixed Fehling's (or 5 ml of Benedict's) for 2 minutes. Red/orange precipitate shows a reducing sugar.
3. **Barfoed's test:** heat 1 ml of sugar solution with 2 ml of Barfoed's reagent in a boiling water bath; note the time for a red precipitate.
4. **Seliwanoff's test:** heat 1 ml of sugar solution with 2 ml of Seliwanoff's reagent in a boiling water bath for 1 minute. Cherry-red colour shows a ketose.
5. **Iodine test:** add 1 drop of iodine solution to a starch suspension. Blue-black colour, disappearing on heating and returning on cooling, shows starch.
6. **Osazone test:** heat 5 ml of sugar solution with about 0.5 g of phenylhydrazine hydrochloride and 0.75 g of sodium acetate in a boiling water bath; note when yellow crystals appear, cool slowly and view under the microscope.

## Observations

| Test | Glucose | Fructose | Sucrose | Lactose | Starch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Molisch | Violet ring | Violet ring | Violet ring | Violet ring | Violet ring |
| Fehling's / Benedict's | Positive | Positive | Negative | Positive | Negative |
| Barfoed's | Red quickly (monosaccharide) | Red quickly | Negative | Slow / negative (disaccharide) | Negative |
| Seliwanoff's | Faint / slow | Cherry red within about 1 minute | Positive slowly (contains fructose, hydrolysed in HCl) | Negative | Negative |
| Iodine | No colour | No colour | No colour | No colour | Blue-black |
| Osazone | Needle-shaped yellow crystals, forms in a few minutes while hot | Same needles as glucose, forms faster | No osazone (unless hydrolysed) | "Powder-puff / cotton-ball" crystals, form on cooling | — |

**Worked record (example).** White sweet powder, chars on heating with burnt-sugar smell; Molisch positive; Fehling's positive; Barfoed's red within 2 minutes; Seliwanoff's faint only after long heating; needle-shaped osazone formed hot → **glucose**.

## Result

The given carbohydrate is ___.

## Precautions

1. Pour conc. H2SO4 gently so that the two layers do not mix in the Molisch test.
2. Do not overheat in Barfoed's test; disaccharides can then give a false positive.
3. Seliwanoff's test must be timed; prolonged heating makes aldoses react too.
4. Phenylhydrazine is toxic; avoid skin contact.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is sucrose non-reducing?** Its glycosidic bond joins the reducing ends of both glucose and fructose, so no free hemiacetal remains.
2. **Why do glucose and fructose give the same osazone?** Osazone formation involves C1 and C2 only, and the rest of the two molecules is identical.
3. **What is the principle of the Molisch test?** Dehydration to furfural derivatives that condense with α-naphthol.
4. **Which test distinguishes glucose from fructose?** Seliwanoff's test (ketose gives cherry red quickly).
5. **Why does the starch–iodine colour vanish on heating?** The helical starch–iodine complex opens up on heating and re-forms on cooling.
6. **What does Barfoed's test distinguish?** Monosaccharides from reducing disaccharides.

# Tests for aromatic hydrocarbons and halogenated hydrocarbons

**Aim:** To identify an aromatic hydrocarbon or a halogenated hydrocarbon in a compound that is insoluble in water, dilute acid and dilute alkali.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Nitrating mixture is highly corrosive; add the compound drop by drop and keep the tube cool.

## Principle

- **Aromatic hydrocarbons** (benzene, toluene, naphthalene) burn with a sooty flame, do not decolourise bromine or Baeyer's reagent (no addition), but undergo **nitration** with conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 to give yellow nitro compounds with a bitter-almond smell.
- **Halogenated hydrocarbons** contain halogen detected by Lassaigne's test. In the **Beilstein test**, the halogen forms a volatile copper halide that colours the flame green. **Alkyl halides** give a silver halide precipitate with alcoholic AgNO3 on warming (SN1 ionisation); **aryl halides** (chlorobenzene) and vinyl halides do not, because their C–X bond has partial double-bond character.

```text
   C6H6 + HNO3 ──conc. H2SO4──▶ C6H5NO2 (yellow, bitter almond) + H2O
   R–X + AgNO3 (alcoholic) ──warm──▶ R–ONO2 + AgX↓
```

## Requirements

Unknown compound, porcelain tile, conc. HNO3, conc. H2SO4, copper wire, 2% alcoholic AgNO3, Lassaigne's extract, test tubes, water bath, beaker of cold water.

## Procedure

**Aromatic hydrocarbons**

1. **Ignition:** a sooty, smoky flame indicates an aromatic compound.
2. **Unsaturation:** no change with bromine in CCl4 or Baeyer's reagent (rules out alkenes).
3. **Nitration test:** add 0.5 ml of the compound drop by drop to a cooled mixture of 1 ml conc. HNO3 and 1 ml conc. H2SO4; warm gently on a water bath (about 50 °C) for 5 minutes; pour into cold water. A yellow oil or solid with a bitter-almond smell shows an aromatic ring.

**Halogenated hydrocarbons**

4. **Lassaigne's test:** confirm the halogen (see the Lassaigne practical).
5. **Beilstein test:** heat a copper wire loop in a flame until it no longer colours the flame; touch it to the compound and reheat. A **green or blue-green flame** shows a halogen.
6. **Alcoholic AgNO3:** add 2 drops of the compound to 2 ml of 2% alcoholic AgNO3 and warm. A precipitate shows an alkyl (or benzyl) halide; no precipitate suggests an aryl or vinyl halide.

## Observations

| Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ignition | Sooty flame | Aromatic |
| Bromine / Baeyer's | No change | Saturated / aromatic ring |
| Nitration | Yellow product, bitter-almond smell | Aromatic hydrocarbon |
| Beilstein | Green flame | Halogen present |
| Alcoholic AgNO3 | White / yellow precipitate on warming | Alkyl or benzyl halide |
| Alcoholic AgNO3 | No precipitate | Aryl halide (e.g. chlorobenzene) |

**Worked record (example).** Colourless liquid, sweet aromatic odour, sooty flame; Lassaigne's: Cl present; Beilstein green; no precipitate with alcoholic AgNO3; boiling point about 132 °C → **chlorobenzene**.

## Result

The given compound is an ___ (aromatic hydrocarbon / alkyl halide / aryl halide).

## Precautions

1. Keep the nitration temperature low to avoid dinitration and fumes.
2. Clean the copper wire in the flame before the Beilstein test.
3. Beilstein test is not specific: some nitrogen compounds (e.g. urea, pyridine) also colour the flame; confirm with Lassaigne's test.
4. Chloroform and carbon tetrachloride are toxic; handle in a fume hood.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does benzene not decolourise bromine water?** Its delocalised π system resists addition; it prefers substitution with a catalyst.
2. **What is the electrophile in nitration?** The nitronium ion, NO2⁺.
3. **Why is chlorobenzene unreactive towards alcoholic AgNO3?** The C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character from resonance with the ring.
4. **What gives the green colour in the Beilstein test?** Volatile copper halides.
5. **Name a halogenated hydrocarbon used as a local anaesthetic spray.** Ethyl chloride.
6. **Which solubility group do these compounds fall in?** The "inert" group: insoluble in water, dilute acid and dilute alkali, and also in cold conc. H2SO4.

# Melting point and boiling point of organic compounds

**Aim:** To determine the melting point of a solid organic compound by the capillary method and the boiling point of a liquid by Siwoloboff's method.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Heat the paraffin bath slowly and never above its smoking point; hot oil causes severe burns.

## Principle

- **Melting point** is the temperature at which a solid changes to liquid at atmospheric pressure. A pure compound melts sharply, over a range of about 1 °C. Impurities **lower** the melting point and **widen** the range. If an unknown and a known sample are mixed and the melting point does not fall (**mixed melting point**), the two are identical.
- **Boiling point** is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals the external pressure. In Siwoloboff's method, a capillary sealed at the top is dipped open end down in the liquid; air and then vapour escape as bubbles, and when heating stops, the liquid is drawn into the capillary at the moment its vapour pressure falls just below atmospheric pressure — that temperature is the boiling point.

## Requirements

Capillary tubes (sealed at one end), Thiele tube or melting point apparatus, liquid paraffin, thermometer (0–360 °C), rubber band or thread, fusion tube (ignition tube), burner, watch glass, glass rod, pure samples for calibration (e.g. benzoic acid).

## Procedure

**Melting point (capillary method)**

1. Powder the dry sample finely on a watch glass.
2. Press the open end of a capillary into the powder and tap the sealed end on the bench until 2–3 mm of tightly packed solid sits at the bottom.
3. Tie the capillary to the thermometer so that the sample is level with the middle of the bulb.
4. Immerse in the Thiele tube filled with liquid paraffin (keep the open end above the oil).
5. Heat the side arm quickly to about 15 °C below the expected melting point, then slowly (about 2 °C per minute).
6. Record **t1** when the first drop of liquid appears and **t2** when the solid has completely melted.
7. Repeat with a fresh capillary for a concordant value.

**Boiling point (Siwoloboff's method)**

8. Put about 0.5 ml of the liquid in a fusion tube; drop in a capillary (sealed at its upper end) open end down.
9. Tie the fusion tube to the thermometer and heat in the paraffin bath.
10. A slow stream of bubbles first appears (expanding air). Continue heating until a rapid, continuous stream comes out.
11. Remove the flame. Note the temperature at which bubbling stops and the liquid just begins to enter the capillary: this is the boiling point.

## Observations

**Melting point**

| Trial | First liquid t1 (°C) | Complete melting t2 (°C) | Range (°C) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 120.5 | 121.5 | 1.0 |
| 2 | 121.0 | 122.0 | 1.0 |

Mean melting point = 121.5 °C; literature value of benzoic acid = 122 °C → the sample is pure benzoic acid.

**Mixed melting point (worked example)**

| Sample | Melting point (°C) |
| --- | --- |
| Unknown | 121–122 |
| Unknown + authentic benzoic acid (1 : 1) | 121–122 (no depression) |
| Unknown + authentic cinnamic acid (1 : 1) | Melts low and over a wide range |

Conclusion: the unknown is benzoic acid.

**Boiling point**

| Trial | Temperature when liquid enters capillary (°C) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 56 |
| 2 | 56 |

Literature boiling point of acetone = 56 °C.

**Reference values for common unknowns (approximate)**

| Solids | m.p. (°C) | Liquids | b.p. (°C) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phenol | 41 | Acetone | 56 |
| Naphthalene | 80 | Chloroform | 61 |
| Resorcinol | 110 | Methanol | 65 |
| Acetanilide | 114 | Ethanol | 78 |
| Benzoic acid | 122 | Ethyl acetate | 77 |
| β-Naphthol | 122 | Toluene | 111 |
| Urea | 133 | Acetic acid | 118 |
| Cinnamic acid | 133 | Chlorobenzene | 132 |
| Aspirin | 135 | Benzaldehyde | 178 |
| Glucose (anhydrous) | 146 | Aniline | 184 |
| Salicylic acid | 158 | Nitrobenzene | 211 |
| Succinic acid | 185 | Methyl salicylate | 222 |

## Result

The melting point of the given compound is ___ °C. The boiling point of the given liquid is ___ °C.

## Precautions

1. The sample must be dry and finely powdered; pack it tightly.
2. Heat slowly near the melting point (about 2 °C per minute).
3. Use a fresh capillary for every determination; a melted sample may change on resolidifying.
4. Keep the thermometer bulb and sample at the same level, and stir the bath (Thiele tube shape helps convection).
5. Note the boiling point while cooling, when bubbling stops, not while bubbles are still streaming.

## Viva questions

1. **Why does an impurity lower the melting point?** It disturbs the crystal lattice and lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid phase (freezing point depression).
2. **What is a mixed melting point?** The melting point of a 1 : 1 mixture of the unknown with a known sample; no depression means they are identical.
3. **Why is liquid paraffin used in the bath?** It is clear, non-volatile, stable up to about 200–250 °C and does not catch fire easily.
4. **Why does the liquid enter the capillary in Siwoloboff's method?** When the vapour pressure inside falls just below atmospheric pressure, the outside pressure pushes the liquid in.
5. **Why should the heating be slow near the melting point?** So that the thermometer and the sample stay at the same temperature.
6. **How does pressure affect boiling point?** Lower pressure lowers the boiling point (used in vacuum distillation).

# Systematic qualitative analysis of an unknown organic compound

**Aim:** To identify an unknown organic compound by systematic analysis — preliminary tests, element detection, solubility, functional group tests, melting or boiling point, comparison with literature values and confirmation by a derivative. (The syllabus asks for at least five unknowns to be analysed this way.)

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Treat every unknown as toxic and flammable.

## Principle

No single test identifies an organic compound. Each step removes possibilities: preliminary tests suggest aromatic/aliphatic and saturated/unsaturated; Lassaigne's test shows which elements are present; solubility tells whether it is an acid, phenol, base, neutral or inert compound; functional group tests name the group; the melting or boiling point picks one compound from the literature list for that group; and a **solid derivative** with a sharp melting point confirms the identity.

```text
   Unknown
     │
     ├─ 1. Physical state, colour, odour, ignition, unsaturation
     ├─ 2. Lassaigne's test: N, S, halogens
     ├─ 3. Solubility: water → NaOH → NaHCO3 → HCl → conc. H2SO4
     ├─ 4. Functional group tests (choose by steps 2 and 3)
     ├─ 5. Melting point / boiling point
     ├─ 6. Match with literature values for that functional group
     └─ 7. Prepare a solid derivative, find its melting point, compare → confirm
```

## Requirements

All reagents of the preliminary, Lassaigne's, solubility and functional group practicals; melting/boiling point apparatus; reagents for derivatives; tables of melting points of compounds and derivatives.

## Procedure

1. Record the physical state, colour and odour, and perform the ignition and unsaturation tests.
2. Prepare Lassaigne's extract and test for N, S and halogens.
3. Carry out solubility tests in order.
4. Use the results to choose functional group tests:
   - No N, soluble in NaHCO3 → carboxylic acid tests.
   - No N, soluble in NaOH only → phenol tests.
   - N present, soluble in dilute HCl → amine tests.
   - N present, neutral → amide, urea, anilide or nitro tests.
   - Neutral, no N, soluble in conc. H2SO4 → carbonyl, alcohol, ester tests.
   - Neutral, sweet, chars → carbohydrate tests.
   - Inert → aromatic hydrocarbon or halide tests.
5. Determine the melting point (solid) or boiling point (liquid).
6. Short-list compounds of that functional group whose literature value is within about 2–3 °C of yours.
7. Prepare a suitable solid derivative (see the solid derivatives practical), purify it and find its melting point; the compound whose derivative matches is the answer.

## Observations and inference (worked example)

| Experiment | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State, colour, odour | White crystalline solid, odourless | — |
| Ignition | Sooty flame, no residue | Aromatic, not a salt |
| Bromine in CCl4 | No decolourisation | No C=C in side chain |
| Lassaigne's test | No N, S or halogen | Contains C, H, (O) only |
| Water | Sparingly soluble in cold, soluble in hot | Polar, small aromatic |
| 5% NaHCO3 | Dissolves with brisk effervescence | Carboxylic acid |
| Ester test | Fruity odour | Carboxylic acid confirmed |
| Neutral FeCl3 | Buff precipitate | Benzoate |
| Melting point | 121–122 °C | Benzoic acid (lit. 122 °C) |
| Derivative: amide (via acid chloride + NH3) | Melting point 127–128 °C | Benzamide (lit. 128 °C) |

**Conclusion:** the unknown is **benzoic acid**, C6H5COOH.

**Short-lists for practice**

| Functional group | Common unknowns (m.p. / b.p.) | Useful derivative (m.p.) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carboxylic acid | Benzoic acid (122), salicylic acid (158), cinnamic acid (133), succinic acid (185) | Benzoic acid → benzamide (128) |
| Phenol | Phenol (41), β-naphthol (122), resorcinol (110) | Phenol → tribromophenol (95) or phenyl benzoate (69); β-naphthol → benzoate (107) |
| Aldehyde / ketone | Benzaldehyde (b.p. 178), acetone (b.p. 56) | 2,4-DNP: benzaldehyde 237, acetone 126; semicarbazone: benzaldehyde 222, acetone 187 |
| Alcohol | Ethanol (78), methanol (65) | 3,5-Dinitrobenzoate: ethanol 93, methanol 108 |
| Amine | Aniline (b.p. 184) | Acetanilide (114) |
| Amide / anilide | Urea (133), acetanilide (114), benzamide (128) | Hydrolysis products |
| Nitro | Nitrobenzene (b.p. 211) | m-Dinitrobenzene (90) |
| Carbohydrate | Glucose (146), sucrose | Glucosazone (needle crystals) |
| Hydrocarbon / halide | Naphthalene (80), chlorobenzene (b.p. 132), toluene (b.p. 111) | Naphthalene picrate |

## Result

The given unknown organic compound is ___ (name and structure).

## Precautions

1. Use a fresh portion of the unknown for each test; never return material to the stock bottle.
2. Always run the element test before deciding which group tests to do.
3. Dry and recrystallise the derivative before taking its melting point.
4. Report the melting point as a range, and compare with the literature value.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is a derivative prepared?** It confirms identity, because two compounds with similar melting points usually give derivatives with different melting points.
2. **What qualities should a good derivative have?** Easy and quick to prepare in good yield, a crystalline solid with a sharp melting point clearly different from those of other candidates.
3. **Why is Lassaigne's test done before the functional group tests?** It tells you which groups are possible (e.g. no amine tests if N is absent).
4. **How do you distinguish benzoic acid from salicylic acid?** FeCl3: buff precipitate vs violet colour; melting points 122 vs 158 °C.
5. **Why does a compound that dissolves in NaOH but not NaHCO3 suggest a phenol?** Phenols are weaker acids than carbonic acid.
6. **What is meant by literature value?** The accepted melting or boiling point recorded in standard reference tables.

# Preparation of solid derivatives of organic compounds

**Aim:** To prepare suitable crystalline derivatives of organic compounds — the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone of a carbonyl compound, the benzoate and tribromo derivative of a phenol, the acetyl derivative of an amine and the 3,5-dinitrobenzoate of an alcohol — and to confirm the parent compound by the melting point of the derivative.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Benzoyl chloride, acetic anhydride and 3,5-dinitrobenzoyl chloride are lachrymatory and corrosive: use them in a fume hood with gloves.

## Principle

A **derivative** is a new compound made from the unknown by a simple, high-yield reaction of its functional group. It is chosen to be a crystalline solid with a sharp melting point that differs clearly from the derivatives of other candidates. Matching the derivative's melting point with the literature value confirms the identity.

| Group | Reagent | Derivative | Reaction type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Aldehyde / ketone | 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine | 2,4-DNP hydrazone | Addition–elimination (condensation) |
| Phenol | Benzoyl chloride + NaOH | Aryl benzoate | Schotten–Baumann benzoylation |
| Phenol | Bromine water | Bromo derivative | Electrophilic substitution |
| Primary / secondary amine | Acetic anhydride | Acetamide (anilide) | Acetylation |
| Alcohol | 3,5-Dinitrobenzoyl chloride | 3,5-Dinitrobenzoate ester | Esterification |

## Requirements

2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine, conc. H2SO4, ethanol, 10% NaOH, benzoyl chloride, bromine water, acetic anhydride, glacial acetic acid, 3,5-dinitrobenzoyl chloride, pyridine (optional), 5% NaHCO3, conical flasks with stoppers, beakers, Buchner funnel, filter paper, water bath, ice, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

**A. 2,4-DNP hydrazone of a carbonyl compound (acetone or benzaldehyde)**

1. Dissolve about 0.25 g of 2,4-DNP in 1 ml of conc. H2SO4; add 2 ml of water dropwise, then 5 ml of ethanol (Brady's reagent).
2. Dissolve 0.1 ml (or 0.1 g) of the carbonyl compound in 2 ml of ethanol and add it to the reagent.
3. Shake; a yellow to orange-red precipitate forms at once or on standing for a few minutes.
4. Filter, wash with a little cold ethanol, recrystallise from ethanol, dry and find the melting point.

**B. Benzoate of a phenol (Schotten–Baumann reaction)**

5. Dissolve 1 g of phenol (or β-naphthol) in 15 ml of 10% NaOH in a stoppered flask.
6. Add 2 ml of benzoyl chloride, stopper and shake vigorously for about 15 minutes (release pressure now and then) until the smell of benzoyl chloride has gone.
7. Filter the solid ester, wash with cold water, recrystallise from ethanol and find the melting point.

**C. Tribromo derivative of phenol**

8. Dissolve 0.5 g of phenol in 10 ml of water; add bromine water with shaking until the yellow colour just persists.
9. Filter the white precipitate, wash with water, recrystallise from dilute ethanol and find the melting point.

**D. Acetyl derivative of an amine (acetanilide from aniline)**

10. Mix 2 ml of aniline with 2 ml of glacial acetic acid and 2 ml of acetic anhydride in a dry flask; warm on a water bath for about 10 minutes.
11. Pour into 30 ml of ice-cold water with stirring; white crystals of acetanilide separate.
12. Filter, recrystallise from hot water, dry and find the melting point.

**E. 3,5-Dinitrobenzoate of an alcohol**

13. Warm 0.5 g of 3,5-dinitrobenzoyl chloride with 0.5 ml of the dry alcohol (and a drop of pyridine) on a water bath for about 5 minutes.
14. Cool, add 10 ml of 5% NaHCO3 to remove 3,5-dinitrobenzoic acid, and stir until the ester solidifies.
15. Filter, wash with water, recrystallise from ethanol, dry and find the melting point.

**Reactions**

```text
A   (CH3)2C=O + H2N–NH–C6H3(NO2)2 → (CH3)2C=N–NH–C6H3(NO2)2 + H2O
B   C6H5OH + C6H5COCl + NaOH → C6H5COOC6H5 (phenyl benzoate) + NaCl + H2O
C   C6H5OH + 3 Br2 → 2,4,6-Br3C6H2OH↓ + 3 HBr
D   C6H5NH2 + (CH3CO)2O → C6H5NHCOCH3 (acetanilide) + CH3COOH
E   C2H5OH + (O2N)2C6H3COCl → (O2N)2C6H3COOC2H5 + HCl
```

## Observations

| Parent compound | Derivative | Observed m.p. (°C) | Literature m.p. (°C, approximate) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acetone | 2,4-DNP hydrazone (yellow-orange) | ___ | 126 |
| Benzaldehyde | 2,4-DNP hydrazone (orange-red) | ___ | 237 |
| Phenol | Phenyl benzoate | ___ | 69 |
| β-Naphthol | β-Naphthyl benzoate | ___ | 107 |
| Phenol | 2,4,6-Tribromophenol | ___ | 95 |
| Aniline | Acetanilide | ___ | 114 |
| Ethanol | Ethyl 3,5-dinitrobenzoate | ___ | 93 |
| Methanol | Methyl 3,5-dinitrobenzoate | ___ | 108 |

**Yield calculation (worked example, acetanilide).** Aniline 2 ml × density 1.02 g/ml = 2.04 g = 2.04/93 = 0.0219 mol. Theoretical acetanilide = 0.0219 × 135 = 2.96 g. Obtained 2.2 g → practical yield = 2.2/2.96 × 100 = **74%**.

## Result

The derivative ___ was prepared; its melting point was ___ °C (literature ___ °C), confirming that the parent compound is ___.

## Precautions

1. Use pure, dry reagents; moisture destroys acid chlorides.
2. In the Schotten–Baumann reaction keep the mixture alkaline and shake thoroughly.
3. Recrystallise every derivative and dry it fully before the melting point.
4. Wash the 3,5-dinitrobenzoate with NaHCO3 to remove the free acid, which would lower the melting point.
5. Work with benzoyl chloride and bromine water in a fume hood.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the Schotten–Baumann reaction?** Benzoylation of phenols, alcohols or amines with benzoyl chloride in aqueous alkali.
2. **Why is NaOH used in benzoylation?** It converts phenol to the more reactive phenoxide and neutralises the HCl formed.
3. **Why are 2,4-DNP hydrazones good derivatives?** They form quickly, are brightly coloured, insoluble and have sharp, distinct melting points.
4. **Why is 3,5-dinitrobenzoyl chloride preferred for alcohols?** Its esters are crystalline solids even for low alcohols that are liquids.
5. **Why is acetic acid added in the acetylation of aniline?** It acts as a solvent and moderates the reaction.
6. **Why should a derivative's melting point differ from that of the parent?** So that the two cannot be confused and possible candidates are clearly separated.

# Construction of molecular models

**Aim:** To build ball-and-stick models of simple organic molecules and use them to study hybridisation, bond angles, conformations and structural (and geometrical) isomerism.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Count the pieces in the kit before and after use.

## Principle

Molecules are three-dimensional. Models show the shapes predicted by hybridisation:

| Hybridisation | Shape | Bond angle | Example | Model piece |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sp3 | Tetrahedral | 109°28′ | Methane, ethane | Carbon ball with 4 holes (tetrahedral) |
| sp2 | Trigonal planar | 120° | Ethene, formaldehyde | Carbon with double bond (two bent springs or a double-bond connector) |
| sp | Linear | 180° | Ethyne | Carbon with triple bond (three connectors) |

Single bonds allow free rotation (conformations); double bonds do not (cis–trans isomers). Isomers with the same formula can be built from the same set of pieces but joined differently.

## Requirements

Molecular model kit: black balls (carbon, 4 holes), white (hydrogen, 1 hole), red (oxygen, 2 holes), blue (nitrogen, 3 holes), green (chlorine, 1 hole); straight sticks for single bonds and flexible springs or connectors for double and triple bonds; protractor.

## Procedure

1. **Methane (CH4):** join four white balls to one black ball. Measure an H–C–H angle; observe the tetrahedron (any two H can be the "front" ones — all equal).
2. **Ethane (C2H6):** join two carbons with one stick and complete with hydrogens. Rotate one carbon about the C–C bond and observe the **staggered** (H atoms as far apart as possible, more stable) and **eclipsed** (H atoms lined up, less stable) conformations.
3. **Ethene (C2H4):** join two carbons with two springs. Check that all six atoms lie in one plane and that the C=C bond cannot be twisted.
4. **Ethyne (C2H2):** join two carbons with three springs; the four atoms lie on a straight line.
5. **Isomers of butane (C4H10):** build n-butane and isobutane (2-methylpropane) from 4 black and 10 white balls; then build the 3 isomers of C5H12.
6. **cis- and trans-But-2-ene:** build both; try to turn one into the other without breaking the double bond (impossible).
7. **Position isomers:** build propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
8. **Functional isomers:** build ethanol and dimethyl ether (C2H6O) from the same pieces.
9. **Cyclohexane:** join six carbons in a ring with single bonds; flip between **chair** and **boat** forms and note the axial and equatorial H positions in the chair.

## Observations

| Model | Shape / feature | Angle | Isomer or conformer observed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Methane | Tetrahedral | 109°28′ | — |
| Ethane | Free rotation about C–C | 109°28′ | Staggered and eclipsed conformations |
| Ethene | Planar, rigid C=C | About 120° | — |
| Ethyne | Linear | 180° | — |
| Butane / isobutane | Different skeletons | — | Chain isomers (2) |
| Pentanes | — | — | Chain isomers (3) |
| But-2-ene | No rotation about C=C | — | cis and trans (geometrical isomers) |
| Propanols | –OH on C1 or C2 | — | Position isomers |
| Ethanol / dimethyl ether | Different connections of O | — | Functional isomers |
| Cyclohexane | Puckered ring | About 109.5° (strain-free) | Chair (more stable) and boat |

## Result

Models of the given molecules were constructed; the observed shapes, bond angles and isomers agree with sp3, sp2 and sp hybridisation.

## Precautions

1. Use the correct ball for each atom (number of holes = valency).
2. Use springs or bent connectors for double and triple bonds.
3. Do not force pieces; broken holes give wrong angles.
4. Dismantle and return all pieces to the kit.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is methane tetrahedral?** Four sp3 orbitals repel equally and point to the corners of a tetrahedron (109°28′).
2. **Why is staggered ethane more stable than eclipsed?** The C–H bonds on adjacent carbons are farthest apart, so torsional strain is least.
3. **Why does but-2-ene show cis–trans isomerism?** Rotation about the C=C would break the π bond.
4. **How many chain isomers does C5H12 have?** Three.
5. **Why is the chair form of cyclohexane more stable than the boat?** All bonds are staggered and there is no flagpole crowding.
6. **What is the shape of ethyne and why?** Linear, because each carbon is sp hybridised (180°).

questions.answer:
1. Definition: isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures, hence different properties.
2. Two main classes: structural (atoms joined differently) and stereoisomerism (same joining, different spatial arrangement).
3. Chain isomerism: different carbon skeleton — C5H12: n-pentane, isopentane (2-methylbutane), neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane). More branching → lower boiling point.
4. Position isomerism: same skeleton and group, different position — propan-1-ol / propan-2-ol; but-1-ene / but-2-ene.
5. Functional group isomerism: different functional groups — C2H6O ethanol / methoxymethane; C3H6O propanal / propanone; C3H6O2 propanoic acid / methyl ethanoate.
6. Metamerism: same functional group, different alkyl groups on either side of –O–, –CO–, –NH– — ethoxyethane / 1-methoxypropane; pentan-2-one / pentan-3-one.
7. Tautomerism: two forms in rapid dynamic equilibrium by proton shift — keto–enol (acetone ⇌ prop-1-en-2-ol; ethyl acetoacetate). Tautomers are real isomers, unlike resonance structures.
8. Ring–chain isomerism: propene / cyclopropane; but-1-ene / cyclobutane.
9. Example of counting: C4H10O has 7 structural isomers (4 alcohols + 3 ethers).
10. Significance: isomers differ in physical properties, reactivity and biological activity.

1. β-Elimination: loss of X from α-C and H from β-C gives C=C.
2. E2: one-step concerted; base removes β-H while X leaves; transition state B···H···C···C···X; rate = k[RX][Base] (second order); needs strong base (alc. KOH, NaOEt); anti-periplanar H and X; no rearrangement.
3. E1: step 1 slow ionisation to carbocation (R3C–Br → R3C+ + Br−); step 2 fast loss of β-H; rate = k[RX] (first order); weak base; polar protic solvent; carbocation may rearrange; competes with SN1.
4. Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° for both; RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
5. Orientation: Saytzeff — more substituted alkene major (2-bromobutane → but-2-ene about 80%); bulky base gives Hofmann product.
6. Comparison table: molecularity, kinetics, steps, intermediate, rearrangement, stereochemistry (anti vs none), base, solvent, isotope effect (E2 shows large deuterium effect).
7. Factors: substrate (3° favours E1), base strength and concentration (strong → E2), solvent (polar protic → E1), leaving group (good LG speeds both), temperature (high favours elimination over substitution).

3. Modern form: addition proceeds through the more stable carbocation (3° > 2° > 1°).
4. Peroxide (Kharasch) effect: with peroxide, HBr adds the opposite way → 1-bromopropane.
5. Initiation: ROOR → 2RO·; RO· + HBr → ROH + Br·.
6. Propagation: Br· + CH2=CHCH3 → BrCH2–C·H–CH3 (2° radical, more stable); radical + HBr → BrCH2CH2CH3 + Br·.
7. Termination: radicals combine.
8. Only HBr: H–Cl bond too strong (H abstraction step unfavourable); I· too unreactive to add to C=C; for HBr both propagation steps are exothermic.

10. Uses: building C–C bonds, cinnamaldehyde, pentaerythritol.

questions.answer:
1. Aldehydes without α-H with concentrated NaOH undergo disproportionation: 2HCHO → HCOONa + CH3OH; 2C6H5CHO → C6H5COONa + C6H5CH2OH.
2. Step 1: OH− adds to C=O → C6H5CH(OH)O−.
3. Step 2 (slow): hydride transfer from this anion to the carbonyl C of a second aldehyde → C6H5COOH + C6H5CH2O−.
4. Step 3: proton exchange → C6H5COO− + C6H5CH2OH.
5. Evidence: in D2O the benzyl alcohol has no C–D bond, so the H came from the aldehyde (hydride transfer).
6. Intramolecular: glyoxal → sodium glycollate.
7. Crossed Cannizzaro: two different aldehydes without α-H; with HCHO, formaldehyde is oxidised to formate and the other is reduced: C6H5CHO + HCHO + NaOH → C6H5CH2OH + HCOONa.
8. Applications: benzyl alcohol preparation; pentaerythritol (CH3CHO + 3HCHO aldol, then crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO) → pentaerythritol tetranitrate (vasodilator).

1. Benzoin: 2C6H5CHO + KCN (catalyst, aqueous ethanol, reflux) → C6H5COCH(OH)C6H5.
2. Mechanism: CN− adds to C=O → C6H5CH(O−)CN; proton shift → carbanion C6H5C−(OH)CN (stabilised by CN and ring); carbanion attacks a second benzaldehyde; proton transfer and loss of CN− → benzoin.
