units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Classification, nomenclature and isomerism

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms four bonds, joins to itself in long chains and rings (catenation), and bonds strongly to H, O, N, S and the halogens. This is why there are millions of organic compounds, and why almost every drug you will study is organic. This unit teaches three basic skills: sorting compounds into families, giving them correct names, and recognising compounds that share a formula but differ in structure (isomers). A short toolkit on electronic effects and reaction intermediates closes the unit, because Units 2–5 use it in every mechanism.

## 1.1 Classification of organic compounds

### By the carbon skeleton

```text
                       ORGANIC COMPOUNDS
                 ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
          ACYCLIC (open chain)          CYCLIC (closed chain)
          e.g. butane, ethanol       ┌──────────┴───────────┐
          straight or branched   HOMOCYCLIC              HETEROCYCLIC
                                 (ring of C only)        (ring has N, O or S)
                              ┌──────┴───────┐       e.g. pyridine, furan,
                          ALICYCLIC      AROMATIC         thiophene
                       cyclohexane,     benzene,
                       cyclopentane     naphthalene
```

- **Acyclic (aliphatic, open-chain)** — carbons in a straight or branched chain. Examples: propane, acetic acid, glycerol.
- **Alicyclic** — carbon rings that behave like aliphatic compounds. Examples: cyclopropane, cyclohexane, menthol.
- **Aromatic (benzenoid)** — contain one or more benzene rings with 6 delocalised π electrons. Examples: benzene, toluene, aspirin.
- **Heterocyclic** — ring contains at least one atom other than carbon. Examples: pyridine (N), furan (O), thiophene (S). Many drugs are heterocycles (nicotine, diazepam, penicillin).

### By saturation

- **Saturated** — only C–C single bonds (alkanes, cycloalkanes).
- **Unsaturated** — at least one C=C or C≡C (alkenes, alkynes, dienes).

### By functional group

A **functional group** is the atom or group of atoms that decides the characteristic reactions of a molecule. Compounds with the same functional group form a **homologous series**.

**Features of a homologous series**

1. Same general formula (alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n−2, alcohols CnH2n+1OH).
2. Neighbouring members differ by –CH2– (14 mass units).
3. Similar chemical properties; physical properties (boiling point, density) change gradually.
4. Prepared by similar general methods.

**Main functional groups**

| Family | Group | General formula | Example (IUPAC / common) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alkane | C–C | R–H | Ethane |
| Alkene | C=C | R–CH=CH2 | Ethene / ethylene |
| Alkyne | C≡C | R–C≡CH | Ethyne / acetylene |
| Alkyl halide | –X | R–X | Chloroethane / ethyl chloride |
| Alcohol | –OH | R–OH | Ethanol / ethyl alcohol |
| Ether | –O– | R–O–R' | Ethoxyethane / diethyl ether |
| Aldehyde | –CHO | R–CHO | Ethanal / acetaldehyde |
| Ketone | >C=O | R–CO–R' | Propanone / acetone |
| Carboxylic acid | –COOH | R–COOH | Ethanoic acid / acetic acid |
| Ester | –COOR' | R–COOR' | Ethyl ethanoate / ethyl acetate |
| Acid chloride | –COCl | R–COCl | Ethanoyl chloride / acetyl chloride |
| Amide | –CONH2 | R–CONH2 | Ethanamide / acetamide |
| Amine | –NH2 | R–NH2 | Ethanamine / ethylamine |
| Nitrile | –C≡N | R–CN | Ethanenitrile / acetonitrile |
| Nitro | –NO2 | R–NO2 | Nitromethane |

## 1.2 Common (trivial) names

Before IUPAC rules, compounds were named from their source or a property: **formic acid** (from ants, Latin *formica*), **acetic acid** (vinegar, *acetum*), **urea** (urine), **wood spirit** (methanol, from wood distillation). Common names are still widely used in pharmacy and in the Indian Pharmacopoeia, so learn both.

**Alkyl group names you must know**

| Group | Structure | Common name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CH3– | methyl | methyl |
| CH3CH2– | ethyl | ethyl |
| CH3CH2CH2– | propyl | n-propyl |
| (CH3)2CH– | 1-methylethyl | isopropyl |
| CH3CH2CH2CH2– | butyl | n-butyl |
| (CH3)2CHCH2– | 2-methylpropyl | isobutyl |
| CH3CH2CH(CH3)– | 1-methylpropyl | sec-butyl |
| (CH3)3C– | 1,1-dimethylethyl | tert-butyl |
| (CH3)3CCH2– | 2,2-dimethylpropyl | neopentyl |
| CH2=CH– | ethenyl | vinyl |
| CH2=CH–CH2– | prop-2-en-1-yl | allyl |
| C6H5– | phenyl | phenyl |
| C6H5CH2– | phenylmethyl | benzyl |

**Prefix meanings in common names**

- **n-** (normal): straight chain, e.g. n-butane.
- **iso-**: a –CH(CH3)2 group at the end of a straight chain, e.g. isobutane (CH3)2CHCH3, isopentane.
- **neo-**: a –C(CH3)3 group at the end, e.g. neopentane C(CH3)4.
- **sec-** and **tert-**: the functional group is on a secondary or tertiary carbon, e.g. sec-butyl alcohol, tert-butyl alcohol.

**Classes of carbon and hydrogen.** A **primary (1°)** carbon is bonded to one other carbon, **secondary (2°)** to two, **tertiary (3°)** to three, **quaternary (4°)** to four. Hydrogens take the class of the carbon they sit on. This idea returns in halogenation (Unit 2) and in SN1/SN2 (Unit 3).

```text
            CH3            1° = carbons a (bonded to 1 C)
            |              2° = carbon c
  a CH3 – C – CH2 – CH3    4° = carbon b
            |
            CH3
   (b is quaternary, c is the CH2, the last CH3 is primary)
```

## 1.3 IUPAC system of nomenclature

The IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) system gives one clear name for every structure. A name has three parts:

```text
     PREFIX(ES)   +   WORD ROOT   +   PRIMARY SUFFIX   +   SECONDARY SUFFIX
   (substituents,     (number of     (saturation:           (main functional
    alphabetical)      C in chain)    -ane, -ene, -yne)      group: -ol, -al …)

   e.g.  2-methyl       but            -an-                   -1-ol    →  2-methylbutan-1-ol
```

**Word roots (1 to 10 carbons)**

| C atoms | Root | C atoms | Root |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | meth- | 6 | hex- |
| 2 | eth- | 7 | hept- |
| 3 | prop- | 8 | oct- |
| 4 | but- | 9 | non- |
| 5 | pent- | 10 | dec- |

### Rules for open-chain compounds

1. **Find the parent chain** — the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the main functional group and as many multiple bonds as possible. If two chains are equally long, choose the one with more substituents.
2. **Number the chain** so that the main functional group gets the lowest locant; then multiple bonds; then substituents (**lowest locant rule**). If there is still a tie, the substituent cited first in alphabetical order gets the lower number.
3. **Name substituents** as prefixes with their position numbers: methyl, ethyl, chloro, bromo, nitro, methoxy.
4. **Use multiplying prefixes** di-, tri-, tetra- for repeated groups (2,2-dimethyl). Every repeat needs its own locant.
5. **Arrange prefixes alphabetically**, ignoring di-, tri-, sec-, tert- (but "iso" and "neo" are counted).
6. **Punctuation**: commas between numbers, hyphens between numbers and words, no space before the root.

### Priority of functional groups (decides the suffix)

When a molecule has more than one group, the highest-priority one becomes the suffix and the rest become prefixes.

| Priority | Group | As suffix | As prefix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Carboxylic acid | -oic acid | carboxy |
| 2 | Sulfonic acid | -sulfonic acid | sulfo |
| 3 | Ester | alkyl …-oate | alkoxycarbonyl |
| 4 | Acid halide | -oyl halide | halocarbonyl |
| 5 | Amide | -amide | carbamoyl |
| 6 | Nitrile | -nitrile | cyano |
| 7 | Aldehyde | -al | formyl / oxo |
| 8 | Ketone | -one | oxo |
| 9 | Alcohol | -ol | hydroxy |
| 10 | Amine | -amine | amino |
| — | Halide, nitro, ether | (prefix only) | halo, nitro, alkoxy |

Learn the short form: **acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine**.

### Worked examples (open chain)

| Structure | IUPAC name | Common name / note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH3 | 2-methylbutane | isopentane |
| (CH3)3C–CH2–CH(CH3)2 | 2,2,4-trimethylpentane | isooctane (fuel standard) |
| CH3CH2–CH(C2H5)–CH2CH2CH3 | 3-ethylhexane | longest chain is 6 C |
| CH3–CH(C2H5)–CH2–CH3 | 3-methylpentane | not "2-ethylbutane" — the ethyl extends the chain |
| CH3–CH=CH–CH3 | but-2-ene | 2-butene |
| CH2=CH–CH=CH2 | buta-1,3-diene | butadiene |
| CH3–C≡C–CH2–CH3 | pent-2-yne | — |
| CH3–CH(OH)–CH3 | propan-2-ol | isopropyl alcohol |
| (CH3)2CH–CH2–OH | 2-methylpropan-1-ol | isobutyl alcohol |
| (CH3)3C–OH | 2-methylpropan-2-ol | tert-butyl alcohol |
| CH2=CH–CH2–CH2–OH | but-3-en-1-ol | –OH gets the lowest number, not the C=C |
| CH3CH2–CO–CH3 | butan-2-one | ethyl methyl ketone (MEK) |
| CH2=CH–CHO | prop-2-enal | acrolein |
| CH3–CO–CH2–CHO | 3-oxobutanal | aldehyde outranks ketone |
| CH3–CH(Cl)–CH2–COOH | 3-chlorobutanoic acid | C of –COOH is C1 |
| CH3–CH(OH)–COOH | 2-hydroxypropanoic acid | lactic acid |
| HOOC–CH2–COOH | propanedioic acid | malonic acid |
| CH3COOCH2CH3 | ethyl ethanoate | ethyl acetate |
| CH3CH2–CO–NH2 | propanamide | — |
| CH3CH2CH2–C≡N | butanenitrile | propyl cyanide; the C of –CN counts in the chain |
| CH3–O–CH2CH3 | methoxyethane | ethyl methyl ether |
| CH3–CH(NH2)–CH3 | propan-2-amine | isopropylamine |
| CCl3–C(CH3)2–OH | 1,1,1-trichloro-2-methylpropan-2-ol | chlorobutanol (Unit 3) |
| CH2(OH)–CH(OH)–CH2(OH) | propane-1,2,3-triol | glycerol |

**How to work an example (3-chlorobutanoic acid):**

```text
   4     3     2     1
   CH3 – CH – CH2 – COOH        1. Main group = –COOH → suffix "-oic acid"
         |                      2. Chain has 4 C (C of COOH counted) → "butan"
         Cl                     3. Number from COOH carbon = C1
                                4. Cl on C3 → prefix "3-chloro"
   Name: 3-chlorobutanoic acid
```

**Common mistakes**

- Choosing a chain that is not the longest (an ethyl group at C2 means the chain is really longer).
- Numbering from the wrong end (always give the functional group the lower number).
- Forgetting to count the carbon of –CHO, –COOH or –CN in the parent chain.
- Writing prefixes in the order of their numbers instead of alphabetically (4-ethyl-2-methyl, not 2-methyl-4-ethyl).

### Carbocyclic compounds (rings up to 10 carbons)

Rules:

1. Add **cyclo-** before the root: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclohexane.
2. A ring with one substituent needs no number: methylcyclohexane, chlorocyclopentane.
3. With two or more substituents, number the ring to give the lowest set of locants; on a tie, follow alphabetical order.
4. If the functional group is on the ring, its carbon is C1: cyclohexanol, cyclohexanone.
5. If a chain has more carbons than the ring, the ring becomes a substituent (cyclohexyl); otherwise the ring is the parent.
6. When –COOH, –CHO or –CN is attached to a ring, use the suffixes -carboxylic acid, -carbaldehyde, -carbonitrile (the carbon of the group is not counted in the ring).

| Structure | IUPAC name |
| --- | --- |
| Cyclohexane ring with –CH3 | methylcyclohexane |
| Cyclopentane with CH3 on adjacent carbons | 1,2-dimethylcyclopentane |
| Cyclohexane with –OH | cyclohexanol |
| Cyclohexane ring with C=O | cyclohexanone |
| Cyclohexanone with CH3 two carbons away from C=O | 3-methylcyclohexan-1-one |
| Cyclohexene with –OH next to the double bond | cyclohex-2-en-1-ol |
| Cyclohexane bearing –COOH | cyclohexanecarboxylic acid |
| Cyclopentane bearing –CHO | cyclopentanecarbaldehyde |
| Cyclopropane on a heptane chain | 1-cyclopropylheptane |

**Benzene derivatives (common names accepted by IUPAC):** toluene (methylbenzene), phenol (hydroxybenzene), aniline (benzenamine), benzaldehyde, benzoic acid, anisole (methoxybenzene). For two substituents, positions are **ortho (1,2)**, **meta (1,3)** and **para (1,4)**: p-nitrophenol = 4-nitrophenol. Ring chemistry itself is covered in Pharmaceutical Organic Chemistry II.

## 1.4 Isomerism

**Isomers** are compounds with the **same molecular formula** but different structures or arrangements, so they have different properties. The word comes from Greek *isos* (equal) and *meros* (parts).

```text
                          ISOMERISM
              ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
     STRUCTURAL (constitutional)          STEREOISOMERISM
     atoms joined differently             same joining, different
   ┌──────┬────────┬───────┬──────┐       arrangement in space
 Chain Position Functional Metamerism  Tautomerism    (geometrical, optical,
                 group                (+ ring-chain)    conformational —
                                                        studied later)
```

### Structural isomerism

**1. Chain (skeletal) isomerism** — different carbon skeletons (straight vs branched).

```text
C5H12:   CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3          n-pentane       (bp 36 °C)
         CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3         isopentane      (2-methylbutane)
         C(CH3)4                  neopentane      (2,2-dimethylpropane, bp 9.5 °C)
```

More branching → smaller surface area → weaker van der Waals forces → lower boiling point.

Number of chain isomers of alkanes: C4H10 = 2, C5H12 = 3, C6H14 = 5, C7H16 = 9.

**2. Position isomerism** — same chain and same group, but the group or multiple bond is at a different position.

- C3H7OH: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
- C4H8: but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
- C3H7Cl: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

**3. Functional group isomerism** — same formula, different functional groups.

| Formula | Isomers |
| --- | --- |
| C2H6O | ethanol (alcohol) and methoxymethane (ether) |
| C3H6O | propanal (aldehyde) and propanone (ketone) |
| C3H6O2 | propanoic acid (acid) and methyl ethanoate (ester) |
| C3H9N | propan-1-amine (1°), N-methylethanamine (2°), N,N-dimethylmethanamine (3°) |
| C4H6 | buta-1,3-diene (diene) and but-1-yne (alkyne) |

**4. Metamerism** — same functional group, but different alkyl groups on either side of a polyvalent group (–O–, –CO–, –NH–, –S–).

- C4H10O ethers: ethoxyethane (C2H5–O–C2H5) and 1-methoxypropane (CH3–O–C3H7).
- C5H10O ketones: pentan-3-one (C2H5–CO–C2H5) and pentan-2-one (CH3–CO–C3H7).

**5. Tautomerism** — two isomers that change into each other rapidly and exist in **dynamic equilibrium**, usually by the shift of a proton and a double bond. The commonest is **keto–enol tautomerism**.

```text
      O                       OH
      ||                      |
  CH3–C–CH3      ⇌      CH2=C–CH3
   keto form               enol form
  (acetone, almost         (tiny amount)
   entirely keto)
```

Tautomers are true compounds (each can sometimes be isolated); resonance structures are not. The enol content rises when the enol is stabilised by conjugation or hydrogen bonding, as in ethyl acetoacetate and acetylacetone. Other types: nitro–aci-nitro and imine–enamine tautomerism.

**6. Ring–chain isomerism** — one isomer is open-chain, the other cyclic. C3H6: propene and cyclopropane. C4H8: but-1-ene and cyclobutane.

### Counting isomers: worked example C4H10O

```text
Alcohols (4):  butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol
Ethers   (3):  1-methoxypropane, 2-methoxypropane, ethoxyethane
Total structural isomers = 7
   chain isomers:     butan-1-ol / 2-methylpropan-1-ol
   position isomers:  butan-1-ol / butan-2-ol
   functional:        any alcohol / any ether
   metamers:          ethoxyethane / methoxypropane
```

C4H9Cl has **4** structural isomers: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

**Why isomerism matters in pharmacy:** isomers can differ in activity, toxicity and stability. Propan-2-ol is used as a skin antiseptic while its isomer propan-1-ol is not; ethanol is a beverage solvent while its isomer dimethyl ether is a gas.

## 1.5 Toolkit for Units 2–5: electronic effects and intermediates

The syllabus scope mentions "intermediates forming in reactions". You will meet these in every mechanism, so learn them now.

### Electronic effects

| Effect | What happens | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inductive (I) | Permanent shift of σ electrons along a chain; fades after 2–3 bonds | –I: –NO2, –CN, –COOH, –F, –Cl, –Br, –OH; +I: –CH3, –C2H5, (CH3)3C– |
| Resonance / mesomeric (R or M) | Delocalisation of π or lone-pair electrons through conjugation | +R: –OH, –NH2, –OCH3; −R: –NO2, –CHO, –COOH |
| Electromeric (E) | Temporary, complete shift of a π pair when a reagent attacks; disappears when the reagent leaves | C=O, C=C under attack (Unit 4) |
| Hyperconjugation | Overlap of a C–H σ bond with an adjacent empty p orbital or π bond ("no-bond resonance") | Explains carbocation and alkene stability (Unit 2) |

Order of +I: (CH3)3C– > (CH3)2CH– > CH3CH2– > CH3–. Order of −I among halogens: F > Cl > Br > I.

### Bond fission and reaction intermediates

- **Homolytic fission** — the bond splits evenly, each atom keeps one electron → **free radicals**. Favoured by light, heat, peroxides and non-polar conditions.
- **Heterolytic fission** — one atom takes both electrons → **ions** (carbocation + anion, or carbanion + cation). Favoured by polar solvents.

| Intermediate | Charge / electrons | Hybridisation and shape | Stability order |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carbocation (R3C+) | Positive, 6 valence electrons | sp2, planar | 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3+ (allyl and benzyl are also very stable) |
| Carbanion (R3C:−) | Negative, 8 electrons | sp3, pyramidal | CH3− > 1° > 2° > 3° |
| Free radical (R3C·) | Neutral, 7 electrons | Nearly planar | 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3· |
| Carbene (:CR2) | Neutral, 6 electrons, two non-bonded | Singlet or triplet | Very reactive; :CCl2 forms from CHCl3 + base |

**Reagents.** An **electrophile** ("electron lover") is electron-poor and attacks electron-rich sites: H+, NO2+, Br+, carbocations, BF3, AlCl3. A **nucleophile** ("nucleus lover") has a lone pair or negative charge and attacks electron-poor carbon: OH−, CN−, Cl−, NH3, H2O, ROH.

**Types of reaction** used in the following units: substitution (Unit 3), addition (Units 2 and 4), elimination (Unit 2), rearrangement (Units 2 and 3) and condensation (Unit 4).

## Remember

- Classify by skeleton (acyclic, alicyclic, aromatic, heterocyclic) and by functional group; a homologous series differs by –CH2–.
- IUPAC name = prefixes (alphabetical) + root + saturation suffix + functional suffix; the main group gets the lowest locant.
- Priority: acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine; halo, nitro and alkoxy are prefixes only.
- Count the C of –CHO, –COOH and –CN in the chain; on rings use -carbaldehyde, -carboxylic acid.
- Structural isomers: chain, position, functional group, metamerism, tautomerism, ring–chain. C4H10O has 7 structural isomers; C5H12 has 3.
- Carbocations and radicals: 3° most stable; carbanions: 3° least stable.

# Unit 2: Alkanes, alkenes and conjugated dienes

This is the heaviest unit of the paper. Alkanes teach you free radical substitution, alkenes teach you electrophilic addition and elimination (E1 and E2), and dienes show what happens when two double bonds talk to each other. Every compound marked with * in the syllabus needs **nomenclature, two methods of preparation, two reactions and uses**; these are given in tables you can copy into an answer.

## 2.1 Alkanes (paraffins)

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, CnH2n+2. The old name **paraffin** means "little affinity": they are unreactive towards acids, alkalis and oxidising agents at room temperature.

### sp3 hybridisation in alkanes

1. Ground state carbon is 1s2 2s2 2p2 (only two unpaired electrons).
2. One 2s electron is promoted to the empty 2p orbital: 2s1 2px1 2py1 2pz1.
3. The 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to give **four equal sp3 hybrid orbitals** (25% s, 75% p character).
4. The four orbitals point to the corners of a regular **tetrahedron**, bond angle **109°28′**.
5. Each sp3 orbital overlaps head-on with a hydrogen 1s orbital (or another sp3 orbital) to form strong **σ bonds**.

```text
                H                     Methane, CH4
                |                     • 4 σ (sp3–1s) bonds
                C                     • H–C–H = 109°28′
              / | \                   • C–H about 1.10 Å
             H  H  H                  Ethane: C–C σ (sp3–sp3) = 1.54 Å
      (tetrahedral: one H points      Free rotation about C–C gives
       towards you, two away)          conformations (staggered, eclipsed)
```

### Preparation of alkanes (two methods)

| Method | Reaction | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wurtz reaction | 2 R–X + 2 Na → R–R + 2 NaX (dry ether) | 2 CH3Br + 2 Na → CH3–CH3; gives even-numbered symmetric alkanes; methane cannot be made |
| Hydrogenation of alkenes (Sabatier–Senderens) | R–CH=CH2 + H2 → R–CH2–CH3 (Ni, about 200–300 °C; or Pt/Pd at room temperature) | Same carbon number as the alkene |
| Decarboxylation | R–COONa + NaOH (soda lime, CaO) → R–H + Na2CO3, heat | CH3COONa → CH4; product has one carbon less |
| Kolbe electrolysis | 2 RCOONa + 2 H2O → R–R + 2 CO2 + 2 NaOH + H2 | Electrolysis of concentrated sodium acetate gives ethane at the anode |
| Reduction of alkyl halides | R–X + 2[H] → R–H + HX (Zn/HCl) | Keeps the carbon number |

### Reactions of alkanes (two important ones + others)

1. **Halogenation** (free radical substitution, see below): CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (UV light).
2. **Combustion**: CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O + heat (fuel use).
3. **Pyrolysis (cracking)**: large alkanes break into smaller alkanes and alkenes on heating (about 500 °C or with catalysts).
4. **Isomerisation**: n-butane → isobutane (AlCl3 + HCl).

### Halogenation of alkanes — free radical mechanism

```text
Initiation    Cl–Cl  ──(hν or heat)──▶  2 Cl·                 (homolysis)

Propagation   Cl·  +  H–CH3   ──▶  H–Cl  +  ·CH3
              ·CH3 +  Cl–Cl   ──▶  CH3–Cl + Cl·              (Cl· is regenerated:
                                                              chain reaction)
Termination   Cl· + Cl·  ──▶ Cl2
              ·CH3 + ·CH3 ──▶ CH3–CH3   (explains traces of ethane)
              ·CH3 + Cl·  ──▶ CH3Cl
```

With excess chlorine the reaction continues: CH3Cl → CH2Cl2 → CHCl3 → CCl4 (all used in pharmacy, Unit 3).

**Reactivity of halogens:** F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. Fluorination is explosive; iodination is reversible (HI reduces CH3I back), so an oxidant such as HIO3 is needed to remove HI.

**Reactivity of hydrogens:** 3° > 2° > 1°, because the radical formed is more stable (3° radical most stable).

```text
Chlorination of propane (room temperature):
  CH3CH2CH3 + Cl2 ──hν──▶ CH3CH2CH2Cl (about 45%)  +  CH3CHClCH3 (about 55%)
  6 primary H × 1.0 = 6.0   :   2 secondary H × 3.8 = 7.6   → 44 : 56 (matches)
Relative rate per H for chlorination: 3° : 2° : 1° ≈ 5.0 : 3.8 : 1.0
Bromination is far more selective (3° H is attacked many hundreds of times faster),
so bromination gives mainly one product.
```

### Uses of paraffins

| Product | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Liquid paraffin (mineral oil) | Lubricant laxative; base of emulsions, cold creams, baby oil |
| Soft paraffin (yellow / white petrolatum) | Ointment base (e.g. simple ointment), emollient |
| Hard paraffin (paraffin wax) | Stiffening agent in ointments; wax baths for joint pain; candles |
| Light petroleum (petroleum ether) | Extraction solvent for fixed oils and alkaloid bases |
| Methane, propane, butane | Fuels (CNG, LPG); butane and propane as aerosol propellants |

## 2.2 Alkenes (olefins)

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with one C=C, CnH2n. "Olefin" means "oil forming", because ethylene adds chlorine to give an oily liquid (1,2-dichloroethane).

### sp2 hybridisation in alkenes

1. Each double-bonded carbon mixes 2s with two 2p orbitals → **three sp2 orbitals** in one plane at **120°**; one 2p orbital stays unhybridised, perpendicular to the plane.
2. sp2–sp2 overlap gives the C–C **σ bond**; sp2–1s overlaps give the C–H bonds.
3. The two unhybridised p orbitals overlap **sideways** → **π bond**, with electron density above and below the plane.

```text
          p                 p
          ●                 ●          π cloud above
     H    |                 |    H
       \  |                 |  /
         C ═════════════════ C          σ bond along the axis (C=C 1.34 Å)
       /  |                 |  \
     H    |                 |    H
          ●                 ●          π cloud below
   All six atoms lie in one plane, angles about 120°.
```

**Consequences of the π bond:**

- The π bond is weaker than the σ bond (C=C ≈ 146 kcal/mol, which is less than twice the C–C single bond ≈ 83 kcal/mol), so alkenes undergo **addition** easily.
- The exposed π electrons attract **electrophiles**.
- Rotation about C=C would break the π overlap, so rotation is restricted → **geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism** (e.g. cis- and trans-but-2-ene).

### Stability of alkenes

Stability is measured by the **heat of hydrogenation** (heat released when one mole adds H2). Less heat released = more stable alkene.

| Alkene | Substitution | Heat of hydrogenation (kcal/mol) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ethene | none | 32.8 |
| Propene | mono | 30.1 |
| But-1-ene | mono | 30.3 |
| cis-But-2-ene | di | 28.6 |
| 2-Methylpropene | di | 28.4 |
| trans-But-2-ene | di | 27.6 |
| 2-Methylbut-2-ene | tri | 26.9 |
| 2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene | tetra | 26.6 |

**Order of stability:** R2C=CR2 > R2C=CHR > R2C=CH2 ≈ RCH=CHR (trans > cis) > RCH=CH2 > CH2=CH2.

Why: (1) **hyperconjugation** — more alkyl groups give more α C–H bonds that share electrons with the π bond; (2) alkyl groups push electrons (+I) and the sp2 carbon is a better partner for them; (3) **trans** is more stable than **cis** because the two groups are far apart (less crowding).

### Preparation of alkenes (two methods)

| Method | Reaction | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dehydration of alcohols | CH3CH2OH ──conc. H2SO4, 170 °C──▶ CH2=CH2 + H2O (or Al2O3, about 350 °C) | Ease: 3° > 2° > 1°; follows Saytzeff; carbocation may rearrange (E1) |
| Dehydrohalogenation | CH3CH2CH2Br + KOH (alcoholic) ──heat──▶ CH3CH=CH2 + KBr + H2O | β-elimination by E2; Saytzeff product major |
| Dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides | BrCH2–CH2Br + Zn ──▶ CH2=CH2 + ZnBr2 | Used to protect/regenerate C=C |
| Partial reduction of alkynes | R–C≡C–R + H2 (Lindlar's catalyst) → cis-alkene; Na in liquid NH3 → trans-alkene | Stereoselective |

### Reactions of alkenes (summary)

| Reagent | Product | Type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H2 / Ni or Pt | Alkane | Catalytic addition |
| Br2 in CCl4 | Vicinal dibromide (red-brown colour disappears: test for unsaturation) | Electrophilic addition (anti) |
| HX | Alkyl halide (Markownikoff) | Electrophilic addition |
| HBr + peroxide | Alkyl bromide (anti-Markownikoff) | Free radical addition |
| H2O / H2SO4 | Alcohol (Markownikoff) | Acid-catalysed hydration |
| Cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 (Baeyer's reagent) | 1,2-Diol (glycol); purple colour lost, brown MnO2 forms | Oxidation (test for unsaturation) |
| O3, then Zn / H2O | Aldehydes and/or ketones | Ozonolysis |
| Heat, pressure, catalyst | Polymer (polythene, PVC, PTFE) | Polymerisation |

## 2.3 Electrophilic addition and Markownikoff's orientation

**Markownikoff's rule:** when an unsymmetrical reagent (HX, H2O, HOCl) adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the **negative part** of the reagent goes to the **carbon that carries fewer hydrogens** (the more substituted carbon).

**Mechanism (propene + HBr):**

```text
Step 1 (slow) — the π electrons attack H+; the more stable carbocation forms

   CH3–CH=CH2  +  H–Br  ──▶  CH3–C⁺H–CH3   (2°, more stable)   +  Br⁻
                       (not CH3–CH2–C⁺H2, a 1° cation)

Step 2 (fast) — bromide attacks the carbocation

   CH3–C⁺H–CH3  +  Br⁻  ──▶  CH3–CHBr–CH3      2-bromopropane (major)
```

**Modern statement:** electrophilic addition goes through the **more stable carbocation**. Because 3° > 2° > 1° carbocations, the H adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens. The modern statement also explains additions where rearrangement occurs.

**Addition of bromine (anti addition):**

```text
   C=C  +  Br–Br  ──▶  cyclic bromonium ion  ──Br⁻ attacks from the back──▶  trans-1,2-dibromide
   (Br2 is polarised by the π cloud; Br⁺ bridges both carbons; Br⁻ opens the bridge from the opposite face)
   Cyclopentene + Br2 → trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane only.
```

## 2.4 Free radical addition: anti-Markownikoff's orientation (peroxide effect)

In the presence of organic peroxides (ROOR) or light, **HBr** adds to unsymmetrical alkenes in the opposite way: Br goes to the carbon with **more** hydrogens. This is the **Kharasch (peroxide) effect**.

```text
Initiation:    RO–OR ──heat──▶ 2 RO·
               RO· + H–Br ──▶ RO–H + Br·

Propagation:   Br· + CH2=CH–CH3 ──▶ Br–CH2–C·H–CH3      (2° radical, more stable
                                                          than ·CH2–CHBr–CH3, 1°)
               Br–CH2–C·H–CH3 + H–Br ──▶ Br–CH2–CH2–CH3 + Br·

Product:       1-bromopropane (anti-Markownikoff)

Termination:   any two radicals combine (Br· + Br· → Br2, etc.)
```

**Why only HBr shows the peroxide effect:**

- **HCl:** the H–Cl bond is strong, so the step R· + H–Cl → R–H + Cl· is energetically unfavourable.
- **HI:** the I· radical is too weak (unreactive) to add to the C=C, and I· atoms combine to I2.
- **HBr:** both propagation steps are exothermic, so the chain runs.

## 2.5 Ozonolysis

Ozone adds across the C=C to give an unstable **molozonide**, which rearranges to an **ozonide**. Hydrolysis with **zinc dust and water** (zinc removes H2O2 so the aldehydes are not oxidised) gives carbonyl compounds.

```text
   R2C=CHR'  ──O3──▶  ozonide  ──Zn / H2O──▶  R2C=O  +  O=CHR'  (+ ZnO)

Examples:
   CH3–CH=CH–CH3 (but-2-ene)     ──▶  2 CH3CHO           (2 acetaldehyde)
   (CH3)2C=CH2 (2-methylpropene) ──▶  (CH3)2C=O + HCHO   (acetone + formaldehyde)
   CH3CH2CH=CH2 (but-1-ene)      ──▶  CH3CH2CHO + HCHO
```

**Use:** locating the double bond. Join the two carbonyl carbons back together with a C=C to rebuild the alkene. This was a classic way of proving structures of natural products.

## 2.6 Elimination reactions: E1 and E2

In a **β-elimination**, a leaving group (X) leaves from the α-carbon and an H leaves from the neighbouring β-carbon, forming a C=C.

### E2 (bimolecular elimination)

- **One step, concerted**: the base removes the β-H while the C–X bond breaks and the π bond forms.
- **Kinetics:** rate = k[RX][Base] — **second order**.
- Needs a **strong base** in high concentration (alcoholic KOH, NaOEt).
- **Anti-periplanar** geometry: H and X on opposite sides, in one plane.

```text
          B:⁻  ↘
                H
                |                                     R        R
          R  –  Cβ  –  Cα  –  R     ──one step──▶      C ═══ C      + B–H + X⁻
                       |                              R        R
                       X  ↘ (leaves at the same time)
   Transition state: B····H····C····C····X  (partial bonds)
```

### E1 (unimolecular elimination)

- **Two steps** through a **carbocation**.
- **Kinetics:** rate = k[RX] — **first order** (only the slow ionisation counts).
- Favoured by 3° substrates, weak bases, polar protic solvents (water, alcohol) and heat. Competes with SN1.

```text
Step 1 (slow):   (CH3)3C–Br  ──▶  (CH3)3C⁺  +  Br⁻
Step 2 (fast):   (CH3)3C⁺  ──base removes β-H──▶  (CH3)2C=CH2  +  H–base⁺
```

### Order of reactivity of alkyl halides

For **both** E1 and E2: **3° > 2° > 1°**.

- E1: 3° carbocation is most stable.
- E2: the more substituted alkene forms, so the transition state is lower in energy.
- Leaving group: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (weaker C–X bond, better leaving group).

### Rearrangement of carbocations

A carbocation may rearrange to a more stable one by a **1,2-hydride shift** or a **1,2-methyl (alkyl) shift**. This only happens in reactions that go through carbocations (E1, SN1, acid-catalysed dehydration and HX addition), never in E2 or SN2.

```text
1,2-Methyl shift (dehydration of 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, conc. H2SO4):

  (CH3)3C–CH(OH)–CH3  ──H⁺, –H2O──▶  (CH3)3C–C⁺H–CH3          2° carbocation
                                          │
                     a CH3 moves with its │ bond pair to the C⁺ (1,2-methyl shift)
                                          ▼
                                    (CH3)2C⁺–CH(CH3)–CH3       3° carbocation (more stable)

  ──loss of H⁺──▶  (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2   2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene (major product)

1,2-Hydride shift: CH3–CH(CH3)–C⁺H–CH3 (2°)  ──H shift──▶  CH3–C⁺(CH3)–CH2–CH3 (3°)
```

### Saytzeff's (Zaitsev's) orientation

**Saytzeff's rule:** when more than one alkene can form, the **more highly substituted alkene** (fewer H on the double-bonded carbons) is the major product.

```text
   CH3–CH2–CHBr–CH3  ──alc. KOH, heat──▶  CH3–CH=CH–CH3  (about 80%, but-2-ene, Saytzeff)
                                       +  CH3–CH2–CH=CH2 (about 20%, but-1-ene)
```

**Evidences / explanation of the rule**

1. **Stability data:** heats of hydrogenation show the more substituted alkene is more stable (but-2-ene 27.6–28.6 vs but-1-ene 30.3 kcal/mol).
2. **Hyperconjugation:** but-2-ene has 6 α-hydrogens against 2 for but-1-ene, so more electron sharing.
3. **Transition state:** in E2 the C=C is partly formed in the transition state, so the factors that stabilise the alkene also lower the energy of the path that leads to it — the more stable alkene forms faster.
4. **Product analysis** of many dehydrohalogenations and dehydrations agrees with the rule.

**Exceptions — Hofmann product (less substituted alkene) forms when:** the base is bulky (potassium tert-butoxide), the leaving group is poor and bulky (quaternary ammonium, –NR3+, Hofmann elimination), or the substrate is crowded.

### Evidences that distinguish E2 and E1

| Evidence | E2 | E1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kinetics | Second order: depends on base concentration | First order: independent of base |
| Isotope effect | Large deuterium isotope effect (C–D breaks slower), so C–H breaks in the slow step | No primary isotope effect |
| Rearrangement | Never | Common |
| Stereochemistry | Anti-periplanar H and X needed (stereospecific) | No special geometry |
| Competition | With SN2 | With SN1 (same carbocation; ratio of products independent of leaving group) |

### E1 versus E2 and factors affecting them

| Factor | Favours E2 | Favours E1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Substrate | 1°, 2°, 3° (3° fastest) | 3° (and 2°, allylic, benzylic) |
| Base | Strong, high concentration (OH⁻, RO⁻) | Weak base or none (H2O, ROH) |
| Solvent | Less polar; alcoholic KOH | Polar protic (stabilises carbocation) |
| Leaving group | Good LG speeds both | Good LG speeds both |
| Temperature | High temperature favours elimination over substitution in both | |
| Rearranged product | Absent | May appear |

**Elimination vs substitution:** alcoholic KOH and heat → elimination (alkene); aqueous KOH at lower temperature → substitution (alcohol). Bulky bases favour elimination.

## 2.7 Conjugated dienes

**Dienes** have two C=C bonds. They are classified by how the double bonds sit:

| Type | Structure | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cumulated (allenes) | C=C=C | Propa-1,2-diene (allene) |
| Conjugated | C=C–C=C (alternate single and double) | Buta-1,3-diene, isoprene |
| Isolated | C=C–(CH2)n–C=C, n ≥ 1 | Penta-1,4-diene |

### Stability of conjugated dienes

1. **Heat of hydrogenation:** buta-1,3-diene releases 57.1 kcal/mol, while two isolated monosubstituted C=C would release about 2 × 30.3 = 60.6 kcal/mol. The **delocalisation energy is about 3.5 kcal/mol**.
2. **Bond length:** the central C2–C3 bond is **1.48 Å**, shorter than a normal C–C (1.54 Å), showing partial double-bond character.
3. **Orbital picture:** all four carbons are sp2; four p orbitals overlap continuously, so the four π electrons are delocalised over C1–C4.
4. **Resonance:** CH2=CH–CH=CH2 ↔ ⁺CH2–CH=CH–CH2⁻ (minor contributor).

```text
   p   p   p   p          continuous sideways overlap over 4 carbons
   ●   ●   ●   ●
   C1==C2––C3==C4         C2–C3 = 1.48 Å (shorter than 1.54 Å)
   ●   ●   ●   ●
   Conformations: s-trans (more stable)  ⇌  s-cis (needed for Diels–Alder)
```

### Preparation of buta-1,3-diene (two methods)

1. **Catalytic dehydrogenation** of n-butane or butenes over a chromium oxide–alumina catalyst at high temperature.
2. **Dehydration of diols**, e.g. butane-1,3-diol or butane-1,4-diol heated with an acid catalyst: HO–CH2CH2CH2CH2–OH → CH2=CH–CH=CH2 + 2 H2O.

**Uses:** monomer for synthetic rubbers (Buna-S, Buna-N, polybutadiene); isoprene units build terpenes, natural rubber and vitamin A.

### Electrophilic addition to conjugated dienes: 1,2- and 1,4-addition

```text
   CH2=CH–CH=CH2  +  HBr

Step 1: H⁺ adds to C1 → allylic carbocation (resonance-stabilised)
   CH3–C⁺H–CH=CH2   ⟷   CH3–CH=CH–C⁺H2

Step 2: Br⁻ attacks either positive end
   attack at C2 → CH3–CHBr–CH=CH2       3-bromobut-1-ene   (1,2-adduct)
   attack at C4 → CH3–CH=CH–CH2Br       1-bromobut-2-ene   (1,4-adduct)
```

| Condition | 1,2-product | 1,4-product | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| About −80 °C | About 80% | About 20% | **Kinetic** — 1,2 forms faster (Br⁻ is nearest C2, and the C2 cation is 2°) |
| About 40 °C | About 20% | About 80% | **Thermodynamic** — 1,4 product is more stable (disubstituted C=C) and the reaction becomes reversible |

Bromine adds the same way: buta-1,3-diene + Br2 → 3,4-dibromobut-1-ene (1,2) and 1,4-dibromobut-2-ene (1,4).

### Free radical addition to conjugated dienes

With HBr and peroxide, Br· adds to the terminal carbon to give a resonance-stabilised **allylic radical**, which picks up H at C2 or C4:

```text
   Br· + CH2=CH–CH=CH2 ──▶ BrCH2–C·H–CH=CH2  ⟷  BrCH2–CH=CH–C·H2
   + HBr ──▶ BrCH2–CH2–CH=CH2  (1,2)   and   BrCH2–CH=CH–CH3  (1,4, usually major)
```

Free radical **polymerisation** of dienes in the same way gives synthetic rubbers.

### Diels–Alder reaction

A **[4 + 2] cycloaddition** between a conjugated diene (4 π electrons) and a **dienophile** (an alkene, 2 π electrons), forming a **cyclohexene ring**. Otto Diels and Kurt Alder received the 1950 Nobel Prize for it.

```text
         CH2                         CH2
       //                          /    \
     HC        CH2               HC      CH2
     |    +    ||     ──heat──▶  ||      |
     HC        CH2               HC      CH2
       \\                          \    /
         CH2                         CH2
   buta-1,3-diene + ethene          cyclohexene
   (two new σ bonds at C1 and C4; new π bond at C2–C3)

   Buta-1,3-diene + maleic anhydride (benzene, warm) → cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylic
   anhydride (a fast, high-yield reaction because the anhydride is an electron-poor dienophile)
```

**Features**

1. **Concerted, one step**, no intermediate; needs only heat.
2. The diene must take the **s-cis** conformation.
3. **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–CHO, –COOR, –CN, anhydride) on the dienophile speed it up.
4. **Stereospecific (syn addition):** a cis-dienophile gives a cis-substituted ring; a trans one gives trans.
5. **Endo rule:** with cyclic dienes the endo adduct is usually the main product.

**Uses:** builds six-membered rings in one step; used in syntheses of steroids, terpenes and many natural products; the reaction with maleic anhydride is a test for conjugated dienes.

### Allylic rearrangement

When a reaction goes through an **allylic cation** (or allylic radical), the positive charge (or odd electron) is shared by the two end carbons. The incoming group can attach at either end, so the **double bond can shift** in the product.

```text
   CH3–CHCl–CH=CH2  ──H2O (SN1)──▶  [CH3–C⁺H–CH=CH2  ⟷  CH3–CH=CH–C⁺H2]
   3-chlorobut-1-ene                         allylic cation

   + H2O ──▶  CH3–CH(OH)–CH=CH2  (but-3-en-2-ol)
          and CH3–CH=CH–CH2OH    (but-2-en-1-ol, the "rearranged" allylic product)
```

The 1,4-addition to buta-1,3-diene is itself an allylic rearrangement. It also occurs in allylic bromination with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS), which goes through an allylic radical.

## Remember

- Alkanes: sp3, 109°28′; free radical halogenation (initiation, propagation, termination); 3° H > 2° > 1°; F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
- Alkenes: sp2, 120°, σ + π; stability rises with substitution (hyperconjugation), trans > cis.
- Markownikoff = more stable carbocation; peroxide effect = HBr only, free radical, anti-Markownikoff.
- Ozonolysis + Zn/H2O → carbonyl compounds; locates the C=C.
- E2: one step, rate = k[RX][B], anti-periplanar, no rearrangement. E1: two steps, rate = k[RX], carbocation, rearrangement. Both: 3° > 2° > 1°.
- Saytzeff: more substituted alkene; bulky base gives Hofmann product.
- Dienes: conjugation energy about 3.5 kcal/mol; 1,2 (kinetic, low temperature) vs 1,4 (thermodynamic, higher temperature); Diels–Alder = diene (s-cis) + dienophile → cyclohexene.

# Unit 3: Alkyl halides and alcohols

Alkyl halides are the classic substrates for **nucleophilic substitution**: SN1 and SN2 are among the most asked 10-mark questions of this paper. Alcohols follow, with their tests and seven pharmaceutically important members. Both families are marked * in the syllabus, so learn nomenclature, two preparations, two reactions and uses for each.

## 3.1 Alkyl halides (haloalkanes)

Alkyl halides have a halogen bonded to an sp3 carbon: R–X (X = F, Cl, Br, I). General formula of monohalides CnH2n+1X.

**Classification**

| Basis | Classes | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number of halogens | Mono-, di-, tri-, polyhalides | CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, CHCl3, CCl4 |
| Carbon bearing X | Primary, secondary, tertiary | CH3CH2Br (1°), (CH3)2CHBr (2°), (CH3)3CBr (3°) |
| Special positions | Allylic, benzylic (very reactive); vinylic, aryl (very unreactive) | CH2=CH–CH2Cl (allyl chloride), C6H5CH2Cl (benzyl chloride), CH2=CHCl (vinyl chloride) |
| Dihalides | Geminal (same C), vicinal (adjacent C) | CH3CHCl2 (1,1-dichloroethane), ClCH2CH2Cl (1,2-dichloroethane) |

**Nomenclature:** common names use "alkyl halide" (ethyl bromide, isopropyl chloride); IUPAC uses the prefix "halo" on the alkane (bromoethane, 2-chloropropane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane).

**The C–X bond** is polar: carbon carries δ+ and halogen δ−, so the carbon is attacked by nucleophiles. Bond strength falls from C–F to C–I, so **R–I reacts fastest** and R–F hardly reacts.

### Preparation of alkyl halides (two methods + others)

| Method | Reaction | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| From alcohols with thionyl chloride (Darzens) | R–OH + SOCl2 ──pyridine──▶ R–Cl + SO2↑ + HCl↑ | Best method: both by-products are gases, so the product is pure |
| From alcohols with HX | R–OH + HCl ──anhydrous ZnCl2──▶ R–Cl + H2O | Groove's process; ease 3° > 2° > 1° |
| From alcohols with phosphorus halides | 3 R–OH + PCl3 → 3 R–Cl + H3PO3; R–OH + PCl5 → R–Cl + POCl3 + HCl | Also PBr3, P + I2 |
| From alkenes | CH3CH=CH2 + HBr → CH3CHBrCH3 | Markownikoff (Unit 2) |
| Halogen exchange (Finkelstein) | R–Cl + NaI ──acetone──▶ R–I + NaCl↓ | NaCl precipitates in acetone, driving the reaction |
| Swarts reaction | R–Br + AgF → R–F + AgBr | Makes alkyl fluorides |

### Reactions of alkyl halides

**Nucleophilic substitution (Nu⁻ replaces X⁻):**

| Reagent | Product | Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aqueous KOH | R–OH | Alcohol |
| NaOR' (Williamson synthesis) | R–O–R' | Ether |
| KCN (alcoholic) | R–CN | Nitrile (one carbon more) |
| AgCN | R–NC | Isocyanide |
| NH3 (excess) | R–NH2 (plus 2°, 3° amines, quaternary salt) | Amine |
| AgNO2 | R–NO2 | Nitroalkane |
| R'COOAg | R'COOR | Ester |

**Elimination:** alcoholic KOH, heat → alkene (Unit 2).

**With metals:** Wurtz (2 RX + 2 Na → R–R) and Grignard reagent (R–X + Mg in dry ether → R–MgX).

## 3.2 SN2 reaction (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution)

**Kinetics:** rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] — **second order**. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate.

**Mechanism — one step, concerted, backside attack:**

```text
   HO⁻ attacks the carbon from the side opposite to Br (backside attack)

            H                          H                           H
            |                          |                           |
   HO⁻  →  C–Br       ──▶     [ HO·····C·····Br ]⁻     ──▶    HO–C      +  Br⁻
          /  \                        /  \                         /  \
       H3C    C2H5                 H3C    C2H5                  H3C    C2H5
   (H, CH3, C2H5 point       transition state: C bonded    the three groups have
    away from HO⁻)           partly to OH and Br; H, CH3,  flipped to the other side
                             C2H5 lie in one plane         (configuration inverted)

   The three groups turn over like an umbrella in a strong wind → inversion.
```

**Stereochemistry:** complete **inversion of configuration** (Walden inversion). An optically active (R)-2-bromobutane gives (S)-butan-2-ol with OH⁻.

**Order of reactivity:** CH3–X > 1° > 2° >> 3° (3° practically does not react by SN2).

Reason: **steric hindrance**. Bulky groups block the backside of the carbon and crowd the five-group transition state. Neopentyl bromide, (CH3)3C–CH2Br, is 1° but reacts extremely slowly for the same reason.

## 3.3 SN1 reaction (unimolecular nucleophilic substitution)

**Kinetics:** rate = k[RX] — **first order**. The rate does not depend on the nucleophile.

**Mechanism — two steps through a carbocation:**

```text
Step 1 (slow, rate-determining) — ionisation
    (CH3)3C–Br  ──▶  (CH3)3C⁺  +  Br⁻
                     planar sp2 carbocation

Step 2 (fast) — nucleophile attacks
    (CH3)3C⁺  +  H2O  ──▶  (CH3)3C–OH2⁺  ──–H⁺──▶  (CH3)3C–OH   2-methylpropan-2-ol
```

**Stereochemistry:** the carbocation is **planar**, so the nucleophile can attack from either face → **racemisation** (a mixture of retained and inverted products). In practice a little more inversion than retention is often seen, because the leaving halide briefly shields one face (ion pair).

**Order of reactivity:** 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3–X, following carbocation stability (+I effect and hyperconjugation of alkyl groups). Allylic and benzylic halides are also very reactive because their carbocations are resonance-stabilised.

**Rearrangement:** since a free carbocation forms, it can rearrange by a 1,2-hydride or methyl shift to a more stable cation, giving rearranged products.

```text
   (CH3)3C–CH2–Br  ──slow──▶  (CH3)3C–C⁺H2  (1°)  ──CH3 shift──▶  (CH3)2C⁺–CH2CH3 (3°)
   neopentyl bromide                                              + H2O → (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3
                                                                    2-methylbutan-2-ol
   (rearranged product, not neopentyl alcohol)
```

## 3.4 SN1 versus SN2

| Feature | SN1 | SN2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Molecularity | Unimolecular | Bimolecular |
| Kinetics | First order, rate = k[RX] | Second order, rate = k[RX][Nu] |
| Steps | Two; carbocation intermediate | One; transition state only |
| Stereochemistry | Racemisation (partial inversion) | Complete inversion (Walden) |
| Substrate order | 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3 | CH3 > 1° > 2° > 3° |
| Rearrangement | Possible | Never |
| Nucleophile | Weak, low concentration is enough (H2O, ROH) | Strong, high concentration (OH⁻, CN⁻, RS⁻, I⁻) |
| Solvent | Polar protic (water, alcohols, formic acid) | Polar aprotic (acetone, DMSO, DMF) |
| Competes with | E1 | E2 |
| Example | (CH3)3CBr + H2O | CH3CH2Br + OH⁻ |

### Factors affecting SN1 and SN2

1. **Structure of the substrate** — steric crowding stops SN2; carbocation stability speeds SN1. 2° halides can go either way depending on the other factors.
2. **Nucleophile** — strength and concentration matter only for SN2. Negatively charged nucleophiles are stronger than their neutral forms (OH⁻ > H2O, RO⁻ > ROH). In protic solvents, nucleophilicity of halides is I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ (large ions are less solvated and more polarisable).
3. **Leaving group** — a good leaving group is a weak base that is stable on its own: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. It speeds both SN1 and SN2. –OH is a poor leaving group; protonating it (–OH2⁺ leaves as water) is why alcohols need acid to react with HX.
4. **Solvent** — polar protic solvents stabilise both the carbocation and the leaving anion by solvation → favour SN1. Polar aprotic solvents dissolve salts but do not hydrogen-bond the anion, leaving the nucleophile "naked" and reactive → favour SN2.
5. **Temperature** — higher temperature favours elimination over substitution.

## 3.5 Structure and uses of important halogen compounds

| Compound | Structure | Preparation (one line) | Uses / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ethyl chloride (chloroethane) | CH3CH2Cl, gas that liquefies easily (bp about 12 °C) | CH2=CH2 + HCl (AlCl3); or ethanol + HCl / ZnCl2 | Spray as a local anaesthetic: rapid evaporation freezes the skin for minor surgery and sports injuries; earlier a general anaesthetic |
| Chloroform (trichloromethane) | CHCl3, heavy sweet-smelling liquid (bp 61 °C) | Ethanol or acetone + bleaching powder (haloform reaction) | Solvent for extraction of alkaloids, fats and resins; preservative (chloroform water); formerly a general anaesthetic, abandoned because it damages liver and heart |
| Trichloroethylene | ClCH=CCl2 | 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane + lime, Ca(OH)2 (loses HCl) | Industrial degreasing and extraction solvent; formerly an inhaled analgesic/anaesthetic (must not be used with soda lime: forms toxic dichloroacetylene) |
| Tetrachloroethylene (perchloroethylene) | Cl2C=CCl2 | Chlorination of trichloroethylene, then removal of HCl | Dry-cleaning solvent; formerly an anthelmintic against hookworm |
| Dichloromethane (methylene chloride) | CH2Cl2, volatile (bp about 40 °C) | Chlorination of methane or chloromethane | Extraction solvent, paint stripper, solvent in coating and in synthesis |
| Tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride) | CCl4, non-flammable | CS2 + 3 Cl2 → CCl4 + S2Cl2 (catalyst); or full chlorination of methane | Solvent for fats, oils and iodine; formerly used in fire extinguishers and as an anthelmintic; now restricted because it is toxic to the liver and depletes ozone |
| Iodoform (triiodomethane) | CHI3, yellow crystals, strong odour (mp about 119 °C) | Ethanol or acetone + I2 + NaOH (or Na2CO3), warm | Antiseptic for wounds (releases iodine slowly), used in dusting powders and dental/ENT packing pastes |

### Chloroform in more detail (often asked)

**Preparation (laboratory, from ethanol and bleaching powder):**

```text
   CaOCl2 + H2O → Ca(OH)2 + Cl2
   CH3CH2OH + Cl2 → CH3CHO + 2 HCl            (oxidation)
   CH3CHO + 3 Cl2 → CCl3CHO + 3 HCl            (chlorination → chloral)
   2 CCl3CHO + Ca(OH)2 → 2 CHCl3 + (HCOO)2Ca   (hydrolysis)
```

**Oxidation in air and light:** 2 CHCl3 + O2 → 2 COCl2 (phosgene, poisonous) + 2 HCl.
**Storage:** dark amber bottles filled to the brim, kept cool; about 1% ethanol is added to convert any phosgene into harmless diethyl carbonate.
**Purity test:** shake with silver nitrate solution — no white precipitate if free of HCl (and therefore of decomposition).

**Reactions:** carbylamine reaction with primary amines (foul-smelling isocyanide, Unit 5); Reimer–Tiemann reaction with phenol (via dichlorocarbene :CCl2); with acetone and KOH gives chlorobutanol.

### Haloform (iodoform) reaction

Compounds containing **CH3–CO–** or **CH3–CH(OH)–** (which is oxidised to CH3CO–) give iodoform with I2 and NaOH.

```text
   CH3–CO–R + 3 I2 + 3 NaOH → CI3–CO–R + 3 NaI + 3 H2O   (α-H replaced by I)
   CI3–CO–R + NaOH → CHI3↓ (yellow) + R–COONa
```

Positive: ethanol, acetaldehyde, acetone, propan-2-ol, butan-2-one. Negative: methanol, propan-1-ol, formaldehyde, pentan-3-one.

## 3.6 Alcohols

Alcohols contain an –OH group on an sp3 carbon. Monohydric alcohols: CnH2n+1OH.

**Classification:** by number of –OH groups — monohydric (ethanol), dihydric/glycols (propylene glycol), trihydric (glycerol), polyhydric (sorbitol); by the carbon carrying –OH — primary (RCH2OH), secondary (R2CHOH), tertiary (R3COH).

**Nomenclature:** replace -e of the alkane by **-ol**: methanol, ethanol, propan-2-ol, butane-1,3-diol, propane-1,2,3-triol.

**Physical properties:** hydrogen bonding between molecules gives high boiling points (ethanol 78 °C against propane −42 °C of similar mass); lower alcohols mix with water because they hydrogen-bond with it; solubility falls as the chain grows.

**Acidity:** alcohols are very weak acids, weaker than or comparable to water (methanol and water both about pKa 15.5–15.7; ethanol about 16). They react with sodium but not with NaOH. Order: CH3OH > 1° > 2° > 3° (alkyl groups push electrons onto the alkoxide oxygen and destabilise it).

### Preparation of alcohols (two methods + others)

| Method | Reaction |
| --- | --- |
| Hydration of alkenes | CH2=CH2 + H2O ──H3PO4, heat, pressure (or H2SO4 then water)──▶ CH3CH2OH (Markownikoff) |
| Hydrolysis of alkyl halides | R–X + KOH (aqueous) → R–OH + KX |
| Reduction of carbonyl compounds | Aldehyde → 1° alcohol; ketone → 2° alcohol (NaBH4, LiAlH4, or H2/Ni) |
| Grignard reagent + carbonyl | HCHO → 1°; other aldehydes → 2°; ketones → 3° alcohol (after hydrolysis) |
| Fermentation | Sugars → ethanol + CO2 (yeast enzymes) |

### Reactions of alcohols

| Reaction | Equation / result |
| --- | --- |
| With sodium | 2 R–OH + 2 Na → 2 R–ONa + H2↑ (acidic nature) |
| Esterification | R–OH + R'COOH ⇌ R'COOR + H2O (conc. H2SO4); fruity smell |
| With HX / PCl5 / SOCl2 | R–OH → R–X |
| Dehydration | Conc. H2SO4 or Al2O3, heat → alkene (higher temperature) or ether (lower temperature, excess alcohol) |
| Oxidation (K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4) | 1° → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; 2° → ketone; 3° resists (only breaks under drastic conditions) |
| Dehydrogenation over Cu at about 300 °C | 1° → aldehyde; 2° → ketone; 3° → alkene (dehydration) |

### Qualitative tests for alcohols

| Test | Reagent and observation | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium metal | Effervescence of H2 (dry sample) | –OH group |
| Ceric ammonium nitrate | Yellow solution turns red | Alcoholic –OH |
| Ester test | Warm with acetic acid + conc. H2SO4, pour into water: fruity smell | Alcohol |
| Lucas test (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2) | 3°: turbidity at once; 2°: within about 5 minutes; 1°: no turbidity at room temperature | 1°, 2°, 3° class |
| Chromic acid (Jones) | Orange colour changes to green/blue-green | 1° or 2° alcohol (3° negative) |
| Iodoform | Yellow CHI3 precipitate | CH3CH(OH)– group (ethanol, propan-2-ol) |

Lucas test works because the alcohol forms the chloride by an SN1 path: 3° carbocations form fastest, and the insoluble chloride makes the solution cloudy.

## 3.7 Structure and uses of important alcohols

### Ethyl alcohol (ethanol), CH3CH2OH

- **Preparation:** (1) **fermentation** of molasses: C12H22O11 + H2O ──invertase──▶ glucose + fructose; C6H12O6 ──zymase──▶ 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2. (2) **Hydration of ethylene** with phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure.
- **Grades:** rectified spirit (about 95%, forms a constant-boiling mixture with water so cannot be purified further by simple distillation); absolute alcohol (water removed by azeotropic distillation or drying agents); denatured (methylated) spirit — made unfit to drink with methanol and other additives.
- **Uses:** solvent for tinctures, elixirs and extracts; antiseptic and disinfectant at about 70% (penetrates cells better than absolute alcohol); preservative; vehicle in many oral liquids; fuel.
- **Tests:** positive iodoform test; ethyl acetate odour with acetic acid + H2SO4.

### Methyl alcohol (methanol, wood spirit), CH3OH

- **Preparation:** (1) **from synthesis gas**: CO + 2 H2 → CH3OH (zinc oxide–chromium oxide or copper catalyst, about 300 °C, high pressure). (2) **Destructive distillation of wood** (old method, hence "wood spirit").
- **Toxicity:** oxidised in the body to formaldehyde and formic acid → metabolic acidosis and damage to the optic nerve (blindness); even small amounts can kill. Ethanol (or fomepizole) is used as treatment because it competes for alcohol dehydrogenase.
- **Uses:** industrial solvent, denaturant of ethanol, antifreeze, raw material for formaldehyde.
- **Distinguish from ethanol:** methanol gives a **negative iodoform test**; heated with salicylic acid and conc. H2SO4 it gives the wintergreen odour of methyl salicylate.

### Chlorobutanol (1,1,1-trichloro-2-methylpropan-2-ol)

```text
              OH
              |
   CH3 –– C –– CCl3          prepared by adding chloroform to acetone
              |              in the presence of solid KOH (cold):
             CH3              CH3COCH3 + CHCl3 ──KOH──▶ (CH3)2C(OH)CCl3
```

- White crystals with a camphor-like odour; usually supplied as the hemihydrate.
- **Uses:** antimicrobial **preservative** (about 0.5%) in injections, eye drops and ear drops; mild sedative–hypnotic and local anaesthetic action.
- Note: it is volatile and is partly lost on autoclaving and through plastic containers.

### Cetostearyl alcohol

- A mixture of solid fatty alcohols, mainly **cetyl alcohol** (hexadecan-1-ol, C16H33OH) and **stearyl alcohol** (octadecan-1-ol, C18H37OH).
- **Preparation:** catalytic reduction (hydrogenation) of fatty acids or their esters from vegetable oils or tallow.
- **Uses:** stiffening agent and emollient in creams and ointments; stabilises oil-in-water emulsions; mixed with sodium lauryl sulfate it forms **emulsifying wax** (base of emulsifying ointment and aqueous cream).

### Benzyl alcohol (phenylmethanol), C6H5CH2OH

- **Preparation:** (1) hydrolysis of benzyl chloride with aqueous sodium carbonate or NaOH: C6H5CH2Cl + NaOH → C6H5CH2OH + NaCl. (2) **Cannizzaro reaction** of benzaldehyde (Unit 4).
- A primary alcohol (the –OH is on a CH2, not on the ring), so it is **not a phenol** and gives no violet colour with FeCl3.
- **Uses:** antimicrobial preservative in multi-dose injections; mild local anaesthetic; solvent. Preserved injections should not be given to newborn babies, in whom benzyl alcohol can be toxic.

### Glycerol (glycerin, propane-1,2,3-triol), CH2OH–CHOH–CH2OH

- **Preparation:** (1) by-product of **saponification** of fats in soap making: fat + 3 NaOH → 3 soap + glycerol. (2) **Synthesis from propene** via allyl chloride (high-temperature chlorination) and hydrolysis steps.
- **Reactions:** (1) heated with KHSO4 → **acrolein** (CH2=CH–CHO), sharp irritating smell (acrolein test); (2) with conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 → **glyceryl trinitrate** (nitroglycerin).
- **Test:** borax–phenolphthalein test — the pink colour of borax with phenolphthalein disappears on adding glycerol (glycerol forms an acidic borate complex) and returns on heating.
- **Uses:** humectant (keeps creams moist), sweetener, solvent and vehicle (glycerites, e.g. tannic acid glycerin), laxative suppositories, plasticiser in gelatin capsule shells, emollient; glyceryl trinitrate is used for angina.

### Propylene glycol (propane-1,2-diol), CH3–CHOH–CH2OH

- **Preparation:** (1) hydration of **propylene oxide** with water and a little acid; (2) from propene via the chlorohydrin (propene + HOCl, then hydrolysis).
- **Uses:** cosolvent in injections and oral solutions for poorly water-soluble drugs; humectant; antimicrobial preservative at higher concentrations; plasticiser. It replaces the related **ethylene glycol**, which is toxic and must never be used in medicines (diethylene glycol contamination has caused mass poisonings).

## Remember

- C–X reactivity R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F; SOCl2 gives the purest alkyl chlorides.
- SN2: one step, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion (Walden), CH3 > 1° > 2° > 3°, polar aprotic solvent.
- SN1: two steps, rate = k[RX], carbocation, racemisation, rearrangement, 3° > 2° > 1°, polar protic solvent.
- Good leaving groups are weak bases (I⁻ best); –OH must be protonated to leave.
- CHCl3 → phosgene in air: amber bottle, full, 1% ethanol. Iodoform = haloform reaction of CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)–.
- Lucas: 3° immediate, 2° about 5 minutes, 1° none at room temperature.
- Chlorobutanol = acetone + chloroform + KOH; benzyl alcohol and chlorobutanol are injection preservatives; glycerol gives acrolein with KHSO4.

# Unit 4: Carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones)

Aldehydes and ketones share the **carbonyl group, >C=O**. Its polar double bond makes the carbon an electron-poor target for nucleophiles, and it makes the neighbouring α-hydrogens slightly acidic. Almost every named reaction in this unit is built from those two facts. Expect at least one 10-mark mechanism (aldol, Cannizzaro, benzoin or Perkin) every year.

## 4.1 The carbonyl group

```text
        R                 • Carbonyl C is sp2: planar, bond angles about 120°
          \   δ+   δ−     • σ bond + π bond between C and O
            C ═══ O       • O is more electronegative → C=O is polar (δ+ on C, δ− on O)
          /               • Resonance:  >C=O  ⟷  >C⁺–O⁻
        R' (or H)         • Nucleophiles attack C; electrophiles (H⁺) attack O
```

- **Aldehyde:** carbonyl carbon carries at least one H: R–CHO (formaldehyde HCHO, acetaldehyde CH3CHO, benzaldehyde C6H5CHO).
- **Ketone:** carbonyl carbon carries two carbon groups: R–CO–R' (acetone CH3COCH3, acetophenone C6H5COCH3).

**Nomenclature:** aldehydes end in **-al** (methanal, ethanal, 3-methylbutanal; the CHO carbon is C1); ketones end in **-one** (propanone, butan-2-one, pentan-3-one). Common names: formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, propionaldehyde, butyraldehyde; dimethyl ketone (acetone), ethyl methyl ketone.

### Electromeric effect

The **electromeric effect (E)** is the **temporary and complete transfer** of a shared π-electron pair to one of the bonded atoms, **at the demand of an attacking reagent**. It occurs only in multiple bonds (C=C, C=O, C≡N) and disappears as soon as the reagent is removed.

```text
   −E effect (C=O, nucleophile attacking carbon):
        >C=O   + Nu⁻   ──▶   >C⁺–O⁻ (momentarily)  ──▶  Nu–C–O⁻
        π pair moves AWAY from the atom the reagent attacks (towards O)

   +E effect (C=C, electrophile attacking):
        CH2=CH2 + H⁺  ──▶  H–CH2–C⁺H2
        π pair moves TOWARDS the atom the reagent attacks
```

| Inductive effect | Electromeric effect |
| --- | --- |
| Permanent | Temporary, needs a reagent |
| Partial shift of σ electrons | Complete shift of π electrons |
| Found in σ bonds | Found only in multiple bonds |
| Fades along the chain | Acts only between the two atoms of the multiple bond |

When inductive and electromeric effects oppose each other, the electromeric effect usually wins because it is called up by the reagent at the moment of reaction.

### Preparation of aldehydes and ketones (two methods each)

| Product | Method | Reaction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aldehyde | Oxidation of 1° alcohol | CH3CH2OH + [O] (K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4) → CH3CHO + H2O; distil the aldehyde out at once so it is not oxidised to acid |
| Aldehyde | Rosenmund reduction | R–COCl + H2 ──Pd / BaSO4 (poisoned)──▶ R–CHO + HCl |
| Aldehyde or ketone | Dehydrogenation over copper (about 300 °C) | 1° alcohol → aldehyde; 2° alcohol → ketone (+ H2) |
| Ketone | Oxidation of 2° alcohol | (CH3)2CHOH + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O |
| Ketone | Dry distillation of calcium salts | (CH3COO)2Ca ──heat──▶ CH3COCH3 + CaCO3 (with calcium formate, aldehydes form) |
| Ketone | Hydration of alkynes | CH3C≡CH + H2O ──HgSO4, dil. H2SO4──▶ CH3COCH3 (via the enol) |
| Both | Ozonolysis of alkenes | Unit 2 |

## 4.2 Nucleophilic addition

Because the carbonyl carbon is electron-poor, the typical reaction is **addition of a nucleophile to C and of H (or an electrophile) to O**.

**Base-catalysed mechanism (example: HCN with a little base → cyanohydrin):**

```text
   HCN + OH⁻ → CN⁻ + H2O            (generates the strong nucleophile)

          R                          R                         R
           \                          \                         \
   N≡C⁻  +  C=O   ──slow──▶      N≡C–C–O⁻    ──H–CN──▶    N≡C–C–OH   +  CN⁻
           /                          /                         /
          R'                         R'                        R'
   (Nu⁻ attacks C; sp2 → sp3,     tetrahedral alkoxide      cyanohydrin
    π pair moves onto O)
```

**Acid-catalysed mechanism (weak nucleophiles such as H2O, ROH):** H⁺ first protonates the oxygen, making the carbon even more positive (>C=O⁺H ⟷ >C⁺–OH); then the weak nucleophile adds.

**Reactivity order:** HCHO > CH3CHO > other aldehydes > CH3COCH3 > other ketones > aromatic aldehydes/ketones.

1. **Electronic:** alkyl groups push electrons (+I) and lower the δ+ on carbon; ketones have two.
2. **Steric:** two groups crowd the tetrahedral product more than one group and an H.
3. **Aromatic** carbonyls are stabilised by resonance with the ring, so they react more slowly.

**Important nucleophilic additions**

| Reagent | Product | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HCN (base) | Cyanohydrin R2C(OH)CN | Hydrolysed to α-hydroxy acids (lactic acid from acetaldehyde) |
| NaHSO3 (saturated) | Crystalline bisulfite adduct | Purification and separation of aldehydes and methyl ketones (adduct is decomposed by dilute acid or alkali) |
| Grignard reagent, then H3O⁺ | Alcohols (1° from HCHO, 2° from RCHO, 3° from ketones) | Building carbon chains |
| Alcohol (dry HCl) | Hemiacetal, then acetal | Protecting carbonyl groups; sugar ring structures are cyclic hemiacetals |
| NH2–Z (addition, then loss of water) | >C=N–Z | Crystalline derivatives for identification (table below) |
| Reduction (NaBH4, LiAlH4) | Alcohols | Synthesis |

**Addition–elimination (condensation) with ammonia derivatives:** >C=O + H2N–Z → >C=N–Z + H2O

| H2N–Z | Product |
| --- | --- |
| Hydroxylamine, NH2OH | Oxime |
| Hydrazine, NH2NH2 | Hydrazone |
| Phenylhydrazine, C6H5NHNH2 | Phenylhydrazone |
| 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent) | 2,4-DNP hydrazone (yellow to orange-red precipitate) |
| Semicarbazide, NH2NHCONH2 | Semicarbazone |

These products are crystalline solids with sharp melting points, so they identify unknown carbonyl compounds in the practical.

## 4.3 Aldol condensation

Two molecules of an aldehyde (or ketone) with **α-hydrogen** combine in **dilute alkali** to give a **β-hydroxy aldehyde (aldol)** or β-hydroxy ketone, which loses water on heating to give an **α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound**.

```text
   2 CH3CHO  ──dil. NaOH, cold──▶  CH3–CH(OH)–CH2–CHO  ──heat (–H2O)──▶  CH3–CH=CH–CHO
                                    3-hydroxybutanal (aldol)                but-2-enal
                                                                            (crotonaldehyde)
Mechanism
Step 1  Enolate formation (OH⁻ removes an acidic α-H):
        HO⁻ + H–CH2–CHO  ⇌  H2O + ⁻CH2–CHO  ⟷  CH2=CH–O⁻   (resonance-stabilised enolate)

Step 2  Nucleophilic addition of the enolate to a second molecule:
        ⁻CH2–CHO + CH3–CHO  ──▶  CH3–CH(O⁻)–CH2–CHO

Step 3  Protonation by water:
        CH3–CH(O⁻)–CH2–CHO + H2O  ──▶  CH3–CH(OH)–CH2–CHO + OH⁻   (base regenerated)

Step 4  Dehydration on heating (E1cB through the enolate):
        CH3–CH(OH)–CH2–CHO  ──▶  CH3–CH=CH–CHO + H2O
```

**Why the α-H is acidic:** the carbanion formed is stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl group (negative charge shared with oxygen).

**Ketones:** 2 CH3COCH3 ──Ba(OH)2──▶ (CH3)2C(OH)CH2COCH3 (diacetone alcohol, 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one) ──heat, –H2O──▶ mesityl oxide.

**Compounds without α-H** (HCHO, C6H5CHO, (CH3)3C–CHO) cannot form an enolate and do **not** undergo aldol condensation; with concentrated alkali they give the Cannizzaro reaction instead.

### Crossed aldol condensation

Aldol condensation between **two different carbonyl compounds**. If both have α-H, four products form (two self and two crossed), which is of little use. It is useful when **one partner has no α-H** (so it can only be attacked) and the other has α-H (forms the enolate).

```text
Claisen–Schmidt reaction (aromatic aldehyde + aliphatic aldehyde or ketone):
   C6H5–CHO + CH3–CHO  ──dil. NaOH──▶  C6H5–CH=CH–CHO + H2O
   benzaldehyde (no α-H)               cinnamaldehyde (3-phenylprop-2-enal)

   C6H5–CHO + CH3COCH3 ──dil. NaOH──▶ C6H5–CH=CH–COCH3 (benzalacetone)
   (with two moles of benzaldehyde → dibenzalacetone, prepared in the BP305P practical)
```

Dehydration is easy here because the new C=C is conjugated with the benzene ring.

## 4.4 Cannizzaro reaction

Aldehydes **without α-hydrogen**, heated with **concentrated** NaOH or KOH, undergo **disproportionation**: one molecule is oxidised to the acid salt and the other is reduced to the alcohol.

```text
   2 HCHO + NaOH (conc.) ──▶ HCOONa + CH3OH
   2 C6H5CHO + NaOH (conc.) ──▶ C6H5COONa + C6H5CH2OH
                                 sodium benzoate  benzyl alcohol
Mechanism
Step 1  OH⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon:
        C6H5–CHO + OH⁻  ──▶  C6H5–CH(OH)–O⁻

Step 2  Hydride transfer (slow, key step): the anion pushes its H, with the bond pair,
        onto the carbonyl carbon of a second aldehyde:
        C6H5–C(H)(OH)–O⁻  +  O=CH–C6H5  ──▶  C6H5–COOH  +  ⁻O–CH2–C6H5

Step 3  Proton exchange:
        C6H5–COOH + ⁻OCH2C6H5  ──▶  C6H5–COO⁻ + C6H5CH2OH
```

**Evidence for hydride transfer:** when the reaction is run in D2O, the benzyl alcohol formed has **no C–D bond**; the hydrogen on its carbon came from the other aldehyde molecule, not from the solvent.

**Intramolecular Cannizzaro:** glyoxal, OHC–CHO, with NaOH gives sodium glycollate, HOCH2COONa.

### Crossed Cannizzaro reaction

Two **different** aldehydes without α-H react together. With **formaldehyde** as one partner, formaldehyde is always oxidised (to formate) and the other aldehyde is reduced to the alcohol, because HCHO is the most reactive towards OH⁻ attack.

```text
   C6H5CHO + HCHO + NaOH ──▶ C6H5CH2OH + HCOONa
   (a good laboratory preparation of benzyl alcohol)

   Pentaerythritol: CH3CHO + 3 HCHO (three aldol additions at the α-carbon)
                    → (HOCH2)3C–CHO, then + HCHO + NaOH (crossed Cannizzaro)
                    → C(CH2OH)4 + HCOONa
   Pentaerythritol is nitrated to pentaerythritol tetranitrate (a vasodilator used in angina).
```

## 4.5 Benzoin condensation

Two molecules of an **aromatic aldehyde** combine in the presence of **cyanide ion** (KCN or NaCN in aqueous ethanol, refluxed) to form an **α-hydroxy ketone** (benzoin).

```text
   2 C6H5–CHO  ──KCN, aq. ethanol, reflux──▶  C6H5–CO–CH(OH)–C6H5   benzoin

Mechanism
Step 1  CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon:
        C6H5–CHO + CN⁻  ──▶  C6H5–CH(O⁻)–CN

Step 2  Proton shift from C to O gives a carbanion, stabilised by both –CN and the ring:
        C6H5–CH(O⁻)–CN  ──▶  C6H5–C⁻(OH)–CN

Step 3  The carbanion attacks a second benzaldehyde:
        C6H5–C⁻(OH)–CN + O=CH–C6H5  ──▶  C6H5–C(OH)(CN)–CH(O⁻)–C6H5

Step 4  Proton transfer and loss of CN⁻ (regenerated catalyst):
        ──▶  C6H5–CO–CH(OH)–C6H5 + CN⁻
```

**Why cyanide is special:** it is a good nucleophile, its –C≡N group stabilises the carbanion in step 2 (so the normally electrophilic aldehyde carbon becomes nucleophilic — "polarity reversal"), and it is a good leaving group in step 4.

**Pharmaceutical link:** benzoin is oxidised (HNO3) to **benzil**, C6H5–CO–CO–C6H5; benzil heated with urea in alkali gives the anticonvulsant **phenytoin**.

## 4.6 Perkin condensation (Perkin reaction)

An **aromatic aldehyde** is heated with the **anhydride of an aliphatic acid** (having α-H) and the **sodium or potassium salt of the same acid** to give an **α,β-unsaturated aromatic acid**.

```text
   C6H5–CHO + (CH3CO)2O  ──CH3COONa, about 180 °C, several hours──▶  C6H5–CH=CH–COOH + CH3COOH
   benzaldehyde  acetic anhydride                                    cinnamic acid

Mechanism (outline)
Step 1  Acetate ion (base) removes an α-H from the anhydride:
        CH3CO–O–COCH3 + CH3COO⁻  ──▶  ⁻CH2CO–O–COCH3 + CH3COOH
Step 2  The carbanion adds to the aldehyde carbonyl (aldol-type addition):
        C6H5–CH(O⁻)–CH2–CO–O–COCH3
Step 3  Acetyl transfer to the alkoxide oxygen, then elimination of acetic acid
        gives the unsaturated anhydride C6H5–CH=CH–CO–O–COCH3
Step 4  Hydrolysis on working up with water:
        C6H5–CH=CH–COOH (cinnamic acid) + CH3COOH
```

**Applications:** cinnamic acid and its derivatives; **coumarin** (a fragrance and the parent of anticoagulants such as warfarin) from salicylaldehyde, acetic anhydride and sodium acetate.

## 4.7 Qualitative tests for aldehydes and ketones

| Test | Reagent | Aldehyde | Ketone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,4-DNP (Brady's) | 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine in acid | Yellow/orange precipitate | Yellow/orange precipitate |
| Tollens' (silver mirror) | Ammoniacal AgNO3, warm | Silver mirror or black precipitate (aldehyde oxidised) | No change |
| Fehling's | Fehling A (CuSO4) + Fehling B (Rochelle salt + NaOH), boil | Red Cu2O precipitate (aliphatic aldehydes; benzaldehyde usually negative) | Negative |
| Benedict's | Alkaline copper citrate, boil | Red/orange precipitate (aliphatic aldehydes, reducing sugars) | Negative |
| Schiff's | Rosaniline decolourised by SO2 | Magenta/pink colour returns | No colour (acetone may give a faint slow colour) |
| Sodium nitroprusside | Na2[Fe(CN)5NO] + NaOH | — | Red/wine colour with methyl ketones (acetone) |
| Iodoform | I2 + NaOH, warm | Only acetaldehyde | Methyl ketones (acetone): yellow CHI3 |
| Sodium bisulfite | Saturated NaHSO3 | Crystalline adduct | Methyl ketones form adducts |

## 4.8 Structure and uses of important carbonyl compounds

| Compound | Structure | Preparation | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formaldehyde (methanal) | HCHO; used as **formalin**, about 37–40% solution in water with methanol as stabiliser | Methanol vapour + air over heated silver or copper catalyst (oxidation/dehydrogenation) | Disinfectant and fumigant (rooms, operation theatres); preserving biological specimens; making hexamine and resins (Bakelite, urea–formaldehyde). Polymerises to paraformaldehyde on standing |
| Paraldehyde | Cyclic trimer of acetaldehyde, (CH3CHO)3 (2,4,6-trimethyl-1,3,5-trioxane) | Acetaldehyde + a few drops of conc. H2SO4 at room temperature (depolymerises on warming with dilute acid) | Sedative–hypnotic and anticonvulsant (status epilepticus, rectal or injection); strong smell, partly excreted in breath; attacks many plastics, so glass is used |
| Acetone (propanone) | CH3COCH3, volatile, flammable (bp 56 °C) | Dehydrogenation or oxidation of propan-2-ol; co-product of phenol in the cumene process; dry distillation of calcium acetate | Solvent for resins, fats, gums, nail varnish; extraction solvent; raw material for chloroform, iodoform, chlorobutanol. Excess acetone (ketone bodies) in diabetic urine is detected by Rothera's test (nitroprusside, purple ring) |
| Chloral hydrate | CCl3–CH(OH)2 | Chlorination of ethanol gives chloral (CCl3CHO); chloral + water → chloral hydrate | Sedative–hypnotic; chloral is also a raw material for DDT and, with alkali, gives chloroform |
| Hexamine (methenamine, hexamethylenetetramine) | (CH2)6N4, a cage of 6 CH2 and 4 N | 6 HCHO + 4 NH3 → (CH2)6N4 + 6 H2O | Urinary antiseptic: in acidic urine it slowly releases formaldehyde (given as mandelate or hippurate salts); solid fuel tablets; rubber chemicals |
| Benzaldehyde | C6H5CHO, smell of bitter almonds | Hydrolysis of benzal chloride (from toluene + Cl2 in light); Étard reaction (toluene + CrO2Cl2); obtained from amygdalin of bitter almonds | Flavouring; synthesis of cinnamic acid, benzoin, dyes. Oxidises in air to benzoic acid (store well closed) |
| Vanillin | 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde | From vanilla pods; synthetically from eugenol (clove oil) → isoeugenol → oxidation; from guaiacol; from lignin | Flavouring agent in syrups, tablets and foods; masks bitter tastes. Gives a phenol colour with FeCl3 and a positive aldehyde test |
| Cinnamaldehyde | C6H5–CH=CH–CHO (3-phenylprop-2-enal) | Main part of cinnamon bark oil; Claisen–Schmidt condensation of benzaldehyde with acetaldehyde | Flavouring, carminative, mild antimicrobial; oxidises in air to cinnamic acid |

### Why chloral hydrate is a stable gem-diol

Most compounds with two –OH on one carbon (gem-diols) lose water at once. Chloral hydrate is stable because (1) the strongly electron-withdrawing –CCl3 group (−I) makes the carbonyl carbon so electron-poor that water adds readily and stays, and (2) intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the –OH hydrogens and the chlorine atoms holds the diol together.

```text
          Cl         OH
           \        /
      Cl –– C –– C – H        CCl3–CH(OH)2
           /        \
          Cl         OH
```

### Hexamine structure

```text
   Four N atoms sit at the corners of a tetrahedron; each pair of N atoms is
   bridged by a CH2 group (6 CH2 bridges). Each N is bonded to three CH2 groups.
   (Cage similar in shape to adamantane.)  Formula (CH2)6N4.
```

## Remember

- Carbonyl C is sp2, δ+; nucleophiles attack C. Reactivity HCHO > CH3CHO > acetone; aromatic slowest.
- Electromeric effect: temporary, complete π shift on demand of reagent; −E for C=O with nucleophiles.
- Aldol: needs α-H, dilute alkali → β-hydroxy carbonyl → α,β-unsaturated on heating.
- Crossed aldol works when one partner lacks α-H (Claisen–Schmidt: benzaldehyde + acetaldehyde → cinnamaldehyde).
- Cannizzaro: no α-H, concentrated alkali, hydride transfer; crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO reduces the other aldehyde.
- Benzoin: 2 ArCHO + CN⁻ → ArCOCH(OH)Ar; benzil → phenytoin.
- Perkin: ArCHO + (RCH2CO)2O + RCH2COONa, heat → ArCH=CRCOOH (cinnamic acid).
- Tollens and Fehling and Schiff: aldehydes; nitroprusside and iodoform: methyl ketones; 2,4-DNP: both.
